Overview

Sprint 1 ended yesterday, Sunday, October 25. Your team held its Sprint Review and Retrospective, counted its real velocity and updated its forecast — the numbers of Class 5. Today Sprint 2 starts, and the board that carried your Sprint 1 cards changes its job: it stops being only a to-do list and becomes a measuring instrument. The four lessons of this hour give you the vocabulary and the arithmetic for that: where the Kanban board comes from and what the pull rule is; what WIP (Work In Progress) is and why a team writes a limit on it; the three clocks that every card carries — lead time, cycle time and work item age — with throughput and Little's Law; and the one chart that shows all of it at once, the CFD (Cumulative Flow Diagram), followed by the question your team answers in the studio: Scrum, Kanban or Scrumban for our product?

Nothing in this hour is a metaphor. Every term has a definition from a free, public source — the Kanban Guide (Coleman & Vacanti, edition 2025.5), the Kanban University guide to the Kanban Method, the Scrum Guide 2020 — and every number has a formula you can check with a pencil. Every example comes from Team Menu, the fictional team of Classes 3 to 5, and uses the Sprint 1 dates its board recorded between October 12 and October 25.

One practical note before we start. There is no new lab today. CQ2 (Checkpoint Quiz 2) takes the first 15 minutes of the Team Studio: it covers Classes 3 to 5 (Scrum events and artifacts, INVEST (Independent, Negotiable, Valuable, Estimable, Small, Testable), story points, one velocity computation and one burndown reading) — not today's material. The rest of the studio turns your Sprint 1 board into a Kanban board with WIP (Work In Progress) limits and computes your own flow numbers; those numbers are the first half of Lab 04 — Flow & Digital Business Brief, which opens next Monday, November 2 (feedback date Sunday, November 8). Keep the dates of every card: they are your data.

Today you will be able to:

  1. Explain where the Kanban board comes from — a card on a factory shelf at Toyota — and what changed when the idea moved to knowledge work; name the parts of a board (states, work items, explicit policies, the commitment point and the delivery point) and the pull rule.
  2. Define WIP (Work In Progress), explain with arithmetic why starting everything at once makes everything late, and write a WIP limit as an explicit policy on a column.
  3. Compute lead time, cycle time, work item age and throughput from a table of card dates, apply Little's Law (average cycle time = average WIP (Work In Progress) ÷ throughput), and say when it may be used.
  4. Read a CFD (Cumulative Flow Diagram) — the thickness of a band, the horizontal distance between two bands, a band that widens — write a provisional SLE (Service Level Expectation), and choose between Scrum, Kanban and Scrumban for a given kind of work, in five sentences with reasons.

Syllabus Topic 2 ("WIP (Work In Progress), Lead times"; "Scrum, Agile"). Learning outcomes: LO 1 (Learning Outcome 1 of the syllabus) — understand the concept and utility of Agile methodologies in business applications; LO 3 (Learning Outcome 3 of the syllabus) — understand the foundations of Scrum methodology (today: where Kanban differs from it); LO 4 (Learning Outcome 4 of the syllabus) — apply the methodologies to your own project.

A note on sources. Two free guides use the word Kanban with slightly different vocabularies, and this lecture names which one it follows in each place. The Kanban Guide (John Coleman and Daniel Vacanti, edition 2025.5, kanbanguides.org) defines the four flow measures used in this course — WIP (Work In Progress), throughput, work item age and cycle time — and the DoW (Definition of Workflow). The Kanban University guide to the Kanban Method (David J. Anderson, 2010; kanban.university) gives the six general practices, the commitment point, the delivery point and the word lead time. The Scrum Guide 2020 (scrumguides.org) remains the reference for everything Scrum says. Where this course adds a rule of its own — the counting convention for days, for example — it says so.

Lesson 1 · The board and the pull

0:02 – 0:12 · 10 minutes, then activity 0:12 – 0:17🎞 Slide 6

By the end of this lesson you can

  • Explain what a kanban is in the Toyota Production System — a card that orders replenishment when something is used up — and what changed when the idea moved to knowledge work in 2004–2010.
  • Name the parts of a Kanban board and of its Definition of Workflow: work items, states from started to finished, explicit policies, WIP control, the commitment point and the delivery point.
  • State the pull rule — a card enters a state only when there is a clear signal of capacity — and tell a pull from a push on your own board.

1.1 · A card on a factory shelf

🎞 Slides 7–8

The word kanban is Japanese; Toyota translates it as signboard — a visual card. In the TPS (Toyota Production System), the manufacturing system that Toyota built after the Second World War, a kanban is a card attached to a container of parts. Toyota's own description is one sentence long: a kanban is "a system that conveys information between processes and automatically orders parts as they are used up" (Toyota UK Magazine). When the assembly line takes a box of parts, the card on that box goes back to the process that makes those parts, and that card — and only that card — is the order to make one more box. Nothing is produced until a card says that something was used.

The TPS (Toyota Production System) rests on two pillars, which Toyota's official page names as jidoka (automation with a human touch: a machine or a worker stops when something abnormal is detected) and JIT (Just-in-Time): making only what is needed, when it is needed, in the amount needed (Toyota Motor Corporation). Kiichiro Toyoda formulated JIT (Just-in-Time); Taiichi Ohno built the practical framework for it between the 1950s and the 1970s, and the kanban card is the information system of that framework. Ohno wrote in his 1978 book that the idea came from watching how an American supermarket shelf is restocked: the customer takes what is needed, and the shelf is refilled afterwards, in the quantity taken.

Three properties of that card matter for us today, and all three survive the trip from a factory to a software team. First, work is pulled by consumption, not pushed by a schedule: the downstream process decides when the upstream process produces. Second, the signal is visual and sits on the work itself. Third, the number of cards in circulation is fixed, so the number of boxes between two processes can never exceed the number of cards — the card count is a cap on inventory. That cap is the first WIP (Work In Progress) limit in history, and Lesson 2 is about it.

1.2 · From the factory to knowledge work

🎞 Slides 9–10

Fifty years later the idea was carried into software. David J. Anderson describes, in his own history, the first knowledge-work pull system at a Microsoft group called XIT (the Microsoft group where the first knowledge-work kanban system was built) in 2004, designed with Dragos Dumitriu for a stream of maintenance requests; then, at the company Corbis in 2006 and 2007, a physical card wall with classes of service — the system he presented as the Kanban Method from 2007 and published as a book in 2010 (A Brief History of Kanban for Knowledge Work). The defining difference from the factory is that a software card does not represent a box of identical parts: every card is a different piece of work. What is kept is the pull, the visual signal and the cap on the number of cards.

Two free guides describe Kanban today, and you will meet both. The Kanban University guide to the Kanban Method defines it as "a method for the definition, management and improvement of services that deliver knowledge work" and lists six general practices: visualize; limit WIP (Work In Progress); manage flow; make policies explicit; implement feedback loops; improve collaboratively, evolve experimentally (kanban.university). The Kanban Guide of John Coleman and Daniel Vacanti, edition 2025.5, is shorter and more formal: "Kanban is a strategy for optimizing the flow of value through a process", with three practices — defining and visualizing a workflow, actively managing items in a workflow, improving a workflow (kanbanguides.org). This course takes its measurements from the Kanban Guide and its board vocabulary from Kanban University, and it says each time which one it is using.

One more fact about both guides, and it is the one students most often miss: Kanban prescribes no roles, no events and no artifacts of its own. The Kanban Guide calls itself "the minimal guidance for Kanban"; the Kanban Method's first change-management principle is start with what you do now. Kanban is added to a way of working that already exists — including Scrum — which is why your team can keep its Product Owner, its Sprint and its Review and still run a Kanban board from today.

1.3 · The board: states, items, policies, and two points

🎞 Slides 11–12

A Kanban board is the visible form of what the Kanban Guide calls the DoW (Definition of Workflow), and a board without that definition is only a wall of notes. The Guide requires six elements: (1) a definition of the work items, the units of value that move through the workflow — for your team, the user stories of Lab 03; (2) a definition of when a work item is started and when it is finished; (3) one or more states the items flow through from started to finished — the columns; (4) a definition of how WIP (Work In Progress) will be controlled; (5) explicit policies for how items flow through each state; (6) an SLE (Service Level Expectation), a forecast of how long an item should take from started to finished, which Lesson 4 defines.

Team Menu's board for Sprint 2 has five columns: Backlog · Ready · In progress · Review · Done. Two of the lines between columns have names in the Kanban University vocabulary. The commitment point is where the team decides that it will do the item — here, the moment a card enters Ready; from that line on, the item is a promise, and the lead-time clock of Lesson 3 starts. The delivery point is where the item is usable by the people it was made for — here, the moment a card enters Done, which for Team Menu means all five checks of its DoD (Definition of Done); the clock stops. Between the two points, every column carries its policy written at its top: what must be true for a card to enter, what is done there, and how many cards may be there at once. "Review: a second member compares every entry with the recipe card; at most one card" is a policy; "Review" alone is a label.

Each card carries, besides the story number and its points, two dates — started (the day it entered In progress) and finished (the day it entered Done) — and, until it is finished, the date it entered Ready. Those dates are not administration. They are the raw data of every number in Lessons 3 and 4, and the reason the Companion to this course keeps saying: keep the dates.

1.4 · The pull rule

🎞 Slide 13

On a push board a card moves because the person upstream finished and handed it on; the capacity of the person downstream is not asked, and work accumulates in front of whoever is slowest. On a pull board the person downstream takes the next card only when there is a clear signal of capacity — the Kanban Guide's words are that work on an item starts "only when there is a clear signal that there is capacity to do so" — and the signal is the board itself: an empty slot under the column's limit. Toyota's card and your empty slot are the same signal. The immediate effect of pulling is that waiting becomes visible: cards accumulate in Ready or in Review instead of silently on somebody's desk, and a column where cards accumulate is where the team looks first. Activity 1 asks you exactly that question — on a wall, with sticky notes, in five minutes: where would the work pile up?

Terms to learn

Kanban (card)
In the Toyota Production System, a visual card attached to a container that travels back to the preceding process as the order to make one more — nothing is produced until a card says something was used.
Toyota Production System (TPS)
Toyota's manufacturing system, built from the 1950s on two pillars: jidoka (stop at an abnormality) and Just-in-Time (make only what is needed, when it is needed, in the amount needed).
Pull
Work is produced or started because the downstream process signalled capacity and demand; the opposite of push, where upstream hands work on regardless of capacity.
Kanban Method
David J. Anderson's method (2010) for defining, managing and improving services that deliver knowledge work; six general practices: visualize, limit WIP, manage flow, make policies explicit, implement feedback loops, improve collaboratively and evolve experimentally.
Kanban Guide
The free guide of John Coleman and Daniel Vacanti (edition 2025.5): Kanban as a strategy for optimizing the flow of value through a process; three practices: define and visualize a workflow, actively manage items, improve the workflow.
Definition of Workflow (DoW)
The six elements a Kanban system must define: work items; when an item is started and finished; the states between them; how WIP is controlled; explicit policies per state; a Service Level Expectation.
Work item
One unit of value moving through the workflow — in this course, one user story (or a spike, marked as a different kind of card).
State
One step of the workflow between started and finished; shown as a column of the board.
Explicit policy
A written rule at the top of a column: what must be true for a card to enter, what is done there, and how many cards may be there at once.
Commitment point
The line on the board where the team decides it will do the item (here: entering Ready); the lead-time clock starts there.
Delivery point
The line on the board where the item is usable by the people it is for (here: entering Done, after all Definition of Done checks); the clock stops there.
Kanban board
The visible form of the Definition of Workflow: columns for states, cards for work items, policies and limits written on the columns, two dates on every card.

Activity 1 · Visualization — a wall board · 0:12 – 0:17 · 5 min

🎞 Slide 14

Four columns on the wall or the whiteboard — Ready · In progress · Review · Done — and one team's Sprint 1 cards on sticky notes (the professor's model is Team Menu's board as it was on Thursday, October 15, day 4 of Sprint 1: four stories, fourteen work items).

  1. Two minutes: place every sticky note in the column where it was on October 15. Write the date the card entered that column in its corner.
  2. Two minutes: count the cards per column. Name the column with the most cards, and the column that has been empty the longest.
  3. One minute: answer in one sentence — if nothing changes, where will the work pile up, and who will be waiting?

Keep the picture in your phone: in the studio you rebuild it as your Sprint 2 board, with limits.

Real-life example 1 · Team Menu writes its Definition of Workflow and sets up the Sprint 2 board, Monday, October 26

🎞 Slide 12
The task

Team Menu — in Sprint 2 Sofia is the PO (Product Owner) and Karim the SM (Scrum Master); Amira and Noah complete the team, and all four build — takes the Lab 03 story set and its Sprint 1 Retrospective decision ("a limit of two stories In progress at once, checked at each Daily Scrum from October 26") and turns them into a written DoW (Definition of Workflow) and a five-column board with policies, limits, a commitment point and a delivery point. Then it performs the first pulls of Sprint 2 and refuses one of them. This is the 25-minute board set-up of today's studio.

Relation to the lecture

It applies section 1.2 (Kanban added to the Scrum the team already runs), section 1.3 (the six elements of the Definition of Workflow, the two points, the policies and the two dates on every card) and section 1.4 (the pull rule and what a refused pull looks like). The same board is what your team builds in the studio, and the dates it records during Sprint 2 are the data you will use to practise Part C of the Mid-Term.

The Definition of Workflow (written at the top of the board, six lines).

# Element (Kanban Guide 2025.5) Team Menu's line
1 Work items One card = one user story of Lab 03 (points on the card); a spike is a card with a dashed border and no points.
2 Started / finished Started = the card enters In progress (date written on it). Finished = all five checks of the DoD (Definition of Done) pass and the card enters Done (date written on it).
3 States Backlog → Ready → In progress → Review → Done.
4 WIP control In progress ≤ 2 cards · Review ≤ 1 card · Ready ≤ 3 cards (refilled at the Daily Scrum). Amira owns the count.
5 Explicit policies Ready: ordered by the Product Owner; a card may enter only with its acceptance test written. In progress: a card is taken by a pair, not assigned. Review: a member who did not build it compares every entry with the recipe card. Done: nothing moves in without the five checks.
6 SLE (Service Level Expectation) Provisional until Sprint 2 ends: "a story should be finished within 10 days of being started, about 85 % of the time" — written in pencil, recomputed from real cycle times (Lesson 4).

The commitment point is the line between Backlog and Ready: Sofia orders the Backlog, but the moment she moves a card into Ready the team has committed to it, and its lead-time clock starts. The delivery point is the line into Done: not "coded", not "reviewed", but usable — the five checks.

The cards on October 26. Carried over from Sprint 1: story 4 (the page in French, 3 points), already In progress since Thursday, October 15 — a carried-over card keeps its start date, so on October 26 it is eleven days old. In Ready, in Sofia's order: story 7 (the banner for changes of the day, 2 points) and the one-hour spike on the phone filter that Lab 03 wrote for story 5. In Backlog: story 5 (hide dishes with my allergen, 5), story 6 (Monday-to-Friday view, 3) and the three slices of story 8 (8a sign-in, 8b correction, 8c log). Sprint 2 Goal: a student can read the page in French and see the day's change of menu.

The first pulls, and a refused one. At the Daily Scrum of Monday, October 26, In progress holds story 4 (one card, limit two). Amira pulls story 7 — the second slot. Noah wants to start the spike; the column is full, and the policy says the signal to start is an empty slot, not an idle person. The refused pull produces a conversation, not an exception: Noah pairs with Karim on story 4's French check, which is the oldest card on the board and the one the Sprint Goal needs most. On Wednesday, October 28, story 7 moves to Review (limit one), a slot opens, and the spike is pulled. On Thursday, October 29, story 7 passes its review and enters Done: its two dates read started Oct 26, finished Oct 29.

What the board now shows that the Sprint 1 board did not. A queue in Ready that the Product Owner refills on purpose; a count on In progress that cannot be exceeded without a decision; an old card that is visibly old; and two dates on every card. The studio asks your team for exactly this: columns, limits, policies, the two points, the two dates — on paper or in your tool, both are accepted.

Team Menu, its members and its data are fictional. Your own board and tables must contain no personal information about anyone outside your team (Legal Notice, section 20).

Code example 1 · Kanban board and pull simulator

🎞 Slide 15
The task

Draws Team Menu's five-column Sprint 2 board from its Definition of Workflow — the policy and the limit written on each column, the commitment point and the delivery point marked — places the cards with their dates, then replays the first four days of Sprint 2 as pull requests: each request is checked against the column's limit and either performed (the card moves and gets its date) or refused with the reason. The execution window prints the count of each column after every step.

Relation to the lecture

Every step is one sentence of section 1.3 (the six elements, the two points, the two dates on a card) or section 1.4 (the pull rule and the refused pull); the board it draws is the one of this lesson's real-life example and of today's studio.

Printed copy: the picture shows the example after its last step. The interactive version (buttons, step-by-step log, downloads) is in the HTML page and in 01_code/ex1_kanban_board_pull.html of the companion ZIP.

<!-- TASK: Draws Team Menu's five-column Sprint 2 Kanban board from its Definition of Workflow (limits and policies on the columns, the commitment point and the delivery point marked), places the eight cards of October 26 with their dates, then replays the first pulls of Sprint 2 as requests that are checked against the column limits — performed (the card moves and receives its date) or refused (with the policy that applies). Relation to the lecture: Lesson 1, "The board and the pull" (the board of today's studio; the dates it records are the data of Lesson 3 and of Lab 04). -->
<!DOCTYPE html>
<!-- Root element of the page; lang="en" tells browsers and screen readers that the text is in English. -->
<html lang="en">
<!-- The head holds information about the page (encoding, title, styles); nothing in it is drawn on screen. -->

<title>Example 1 · Team Menu · Kanban board and pull simulator</title>
<!-- Start of the style sheet: each rule below sets how one part of the page looks. -->
<style>
/* Whole page: system font, warm paper background, dark ink text, no outer margin, 14 px base size. */
body{margin:0;font:14px/1.45 system-ui,-apple-system,"Segoe UI",Roboto,Arial,sans-serif;background:#FAF7F2;color:#1B2B2E}
/* Control bar at the top: title and buttons on one row, wrapping onto two rows on narrow screens. */
.bar{display:flex;flex-wrap:wrap;gap:8px;align-items:center;padding:10px 12px;border-bottom:1px solid #DDD3C4;background:#fff}
/* Example title inside the bar: bold, pushes the buttons to the right. */
.bar h1{font-size:15px;margin:0 auto 0 0}
/* Every button: rounded, teal outline, readable size, hand cursor. */
button{font:inherit;font-weight:600;padding:6px 12px;border-radius:999px;border:1px solid #0E7C7B;background:#fff;color:#0A5F5E;cursor:pointer}
/* The Start/Pause button is filled teal because it is the main action. */
button.main{background:#0E7C7B;color:#fff}
/* The two download buttons are quieter (sand background) so the run controls stay the eye-catchers. */
button.dl{background:#F1ECE3;border-color:#C9BDA8;color:#1B2B2E}
/* Visible focus ring for keyboard users. */
button:focus-visible{outline:3px solid #B5440C;outline-offset:2px}
/* Step counter beside the buttons, in a quieter grey with digits of equal width. */
#counter{color:#54646A;font-variant-numeric:tabular-nums}
/* Two columns: visualization on the left, execution window on the right. */
.grid{display:grid;grid-template-columns:1.55fr 1fr;gap:12px;padding:12px}
/* Below 760 px the two columns are stacked so they stay readable on a phone. */
@media (max-width:760px){.grid{grid-template-columns:1fr}}
/* White panels with a thin border and rounded corners. */
.panel{background:#fff;border:1px solid #DDD3C4;border-radius:12px;padding:10px;min-width:0}
/* Small uppercase heading at the top of each panel. */
.panel h2{font-size:12px;letter-spacing:.06em;text-transform:uppercase;color:#54646A;margin:0 0 6px}
/* The drawing scales with the panel and keeps its proportions. */
svg{width:100%;height:auto;display:block}
/* Execution window: fixed height, scrolls, monospaced so the columns of the log line up. */
#log{height:470px;overflow:auto;font:12px/1.5 ui-monospace,SFMono-Regular,Menlo,Consolas,monospace;background:#F6F3EE;border-radius:8px;padding:8px}
/* One log line: small padding and an invisible left border used for highlighting. */
#log div{padding:2px 6px;border-left:3px solid transparent;white-space:pre-wrap}
/* The line of the step that has just run is highlighted. */
#log div.now{background:#E4F1F0;border-left-color:#0E7C7B}
/* End of the style sheet. */
</style>
<!-- End of the head. -->
</head>

<div class="panel">
<!-- Heading of the right panel. -->
<h2>Execution window · every step is written here</h2>

<div id="log" aria-live="polite"></div>
<!-- End of the right panel. -->

];

{ id: "4", title: "The page in French", pts: 3, col: "inprog", committed: "Oct 12", started: "Oct 15", finished: null, spike: false },

{ id: "S5", title: "Spike · phone filter (1 h)", pts: 0, col: "ready", committed: "Oct 26", started: null, finished: null, spike: true },

{ id: "5", title: "Hide dishes with my allergen", pts: 5, col: "backlog", committed: null, started: null, finished: null, spike: false },
// Story 6, a Could have.
{ id: "6", title: "Meals of Monday to Friday", pts: 3, col: "backlog", committed: null, started: null, finished: null, spike: false },

{ id: "8a", title: "Chef signs in (kitchen code)", pts: 2, col: "backlog", committed: null, started: null, finished: null, spike: false },
// Slice 8b.
{ id: "8b", title: "Chef corrects one entry", pts: 3, col: "backlog", committed: null, started: null, finished: null, spike: false },

{ id: "8c", title: "Every correction is logged", pts: 2, col: "backlog", committed: null, started: null, finished: null, spike: false }

];

// Monday: Amira pulls story 7 into the second slot of In progress.
{ day: "Mon Oct 26", who: "Amira", card: "7", to: "inprog", note: "the Sprint Goal needs the banner; slot 2 of 2 is free" },
// Monday: Noah wants to start the spike; the column will be full.

// Tuesday: the Product Owner refills Ready by committing story 5.
{ day: "Tue Oct 27", who: "Sofia (PO)", card: "5", to: "ready", note: "refill at the Daily Scrum; the acceptance test of story 5 is written" },
// Wednesday: story 7 is ready for its second-person check.
{ day: "Wed Oct 28", who: "Amira", card: "7", to: "review", note: "the banner shows above the meals on the test link" },
// Wednesday: a slot opened in In progress, so the spike is pulled.
{ day: "Wed Oct 28", who: "Noah", card: "S5", to: "inprog", note: "a slot opened when story 7 left In progress" },
// Thursday: story 4 is ready for review, but Review still holds story 7.
{ day: "Thu Oct 29", who: "Karim", card: "4", to: "review", note: "the French labels are complete", ifRefused: "Karim and Noah take the review of story 7 themselves, to free the slot (swarming on the oldest work in Review)." },
// Thursday: story 7 passes the five checks and crosses the delivery point.
{ day: "Thu Oct 29", who: "Noah (reviewer)", card: "7", to: "done", note: "all five DoD checks pass" },
// Thursday, later: story 4 enters the freed Review slot.
{ day: "Thu Oct 29", who: "Karim", card: "4", to: "review", note: "Review is empty again" },
// Friday: story 5 is pulled into In progress (the spike reported on Thursday evening: 5 points confirmed).
{ day: "Fri Oct 30", who: "Amira", card: "5", to: "inprog", note: "the spike reported: the filter is a 5; a slot is free since story 4 left In progress" }

];

// Resets the running state (called by Restart).

// x position of the left edge of column i (five columns of 136 px with 10 px gaps, starting at 16).

// Index of a column from its key.
function colIndex(key) { return COLUMNS.findIndex(function (c) { return c.key === key; }); }

// Draws the static board: title, five columns with name, limit and policy, the commitment point and the delivery point.
function drawBoard() {
// Removes everything drawn before (needed by Restart).
svg.innerHTML = "";
// Title of the board.
txt(16, 22, "Team Menu · Sprint 2 board (Oct 26 → Nov 8) · Definition of Workflow on the columns", { size: 13, weight: 700 });
// One column per state.
COLUMNS.forEach(function (c, i) {
// Column background.

// Separator under the header.
el("line", { x1: colX(i), y1: 112, x2: colX(i) + 136, y2: 112, stroke: C.line });
// End of the loop over columns.
});

el("line", { x1: colX(1) - 5, y1: 34, x2: colX(1) - 5, y2: 504, stroke: C.indigo, "stroke-width": 2, "stroke-dasharray": "5 4" });
// Its label, written vertically along the line.

el("line", { x1: colX(4) - 5, y1: 34, x2: colX(4) - 5, y2: 504, stroke: C.teal, "stroke-width": 2, "stroke-dasharray": "5 4" });
// Its label.
txt(colX(4) - 9, 300, "delivery point · both clocks stop", { size: 8.5, weight: 700, fill: C.teal, anchor: "middle" }).setAttribute("transform", "rotate(-90 " + (colX(4) - 9) + " 300)");

}
// Draws every card in its column, stacked from the top, with its dates; a dashed border marks a spike.
function drawCards(highlightId, refused) { const g = parts.cards; g.innerHTML = ""; COLUMNS.forEach(function (c, i) { let y = 120; cards.filter(function (k) { return k.col === c.key; }).forEach(function (k) { const hi = k.id === highlightId; const fill = hi ? (refused ? C.rustT : C.indigoT) : "#fff"; const stroke = hi ? (refused ? C.rust : C.indigo) : (k.spike ? C.muted : C.line); const r = el("rect", { x: colX(i) + 8, y: y, width: 120, height: 56, rx: 6, fill: fill, stroke: stroke, "stroke-width": hi ? 2 : 1 }, g); if (k.spike) { r.setAttribute("stroke-dasharray", "4 3"); } txt(colX(i) + 14, y + 13, "#" + k.id + (k.spike ? "" : " · " + k.pts + " pt"), { size: 9.5, weight: 800, parent: g }); wrap(k.title, 24).slice(0, 2).forEach(function (l, li) { txt(colX(i) + 14, y + 25 + li * 10, l, { size: 8.3, parent: g }); }); const dates = (k.committed ? "R " + k.committed : "") + (k.started ? "  S " + k.started : "") + (k.finished ? "  D " + k.finished : ""); txt(colX(i) + 14, y + 48, dates || "—", { size: 8, fill: C.muted, parent: g }); y += 62; }); }); }
// Tries to move a card into a target column: accepted when the column has no limit or a free slot; the dates are written on acceptance.
function tryPull(req) { const k = card(req.card); const target = COLUMNS[colIndex(req.to)]; const n = countIn(req.to); if (target.limit !== null && n >= target.limit) { state.refused += 1; drawCards(k.id, true); return { ok: false, text: "REFUSED · " + req.day + " · " + req.who + " asks to move #" + k.id + " to " + target.name + " (" + req.note + ") → " + target.name + " holds " + n + " of " + target.limit + ": no free slot, no signal to start. Policy: " + target.policy + "\n     " + (req.ifRefused || "The card stays where it is.") }; } const from = COLUMNS[colIndex(k.col)].name; k.col = req.to; let clocks = ""; if (req.to === "ready") { k.committed = req.day.slice(4); clocks = " Crosses the commitment point: the lead-time clock of #" + k.id + " starts (" + k.committed + ")."; } if (req.to === "inprog") { k.started = req.day.slice(4); clocks = " Start date written: " + k.started + " — the cycle-time clock starts."; } if (req.to === "done") { k.finished = req.day.slice(4); clocks = " Crosses the delivery point: finish date " + k.finished + "; lead time R " + k.committed + " → D " + k.finished + ", cycle time S " + k.started + " → D " + k.finished + "."; } state.performed += 1; drawCards(k.id, false); return { ok: true, text: "PULL · " + req.day + " · " + req.who + " moves #" + k.id + " from " + from + " to " + target.name + " (" + req.note + ") → slot " + (n + 1) + (target.limit ? " of " + target.limit : "") + "." + clocks }; }
// Builds the ordered list of steps.
function buildSteps() {
// Empties the list (needed by Restart).
steps.length = 0;
// Step 1: what the program will do.
steps.push(function () { return "Start · the Definition of Workflow is written, the board is drawn with its limits and policies, the eight cards of October 26 are placed, and the first pull requests of Sprint 2 are checked against the limits one by one."; });
// Step 2: the six lines of the Definition of Workflow.
steps.push(function () { return "Definition of Workflow (six elements, Kanban Guide 2025.5):\n     " + DOW.join("\n     "); });
// Step 3: the cards and the two points.
steps.push(function () { drawCards(null, false); return "Cards placed · " + counts() + " · Backlog 5. Story 4 is carried over: started Oct 15 in Sprint 1, still In progress, 11 days old today. The commitment point sits before Ready (the lead-time clock starts there); the delivery point sits before Done (both clocks stop there)."; });
// Steps 4 onward: one step per pull request.
REQUESTS.forEach(function (req) { steps.push(function () { const r = tryPull(req); return r.text + "\n     Counts: " + counts(); }); });
// Last step: the summary.
steps.push(function () { drawCards(null, false); const done = cards.filter(function (k) { return k.col === "done"; }).map(function (k) { return "#" + k.id + " (R " + k.committed + ", S " + k.started + ", D " + k.finished + ")"; }); return "Done · " + state.performed + " pulls performed, " + state.refused + " refused by a limit — each refusal produced a pairing, not idle time. Finished so far: " + (done.join(", ") || "none") + ". Every card in the limited columns carries its dates: those dates are Lesson 3."; });
// End of buildSteps.
}
// Restart: stops, resets the state, clears the log, redraws the empty board and returns to step 0.
function restart() { pause(); next = 0; resetState(); logBox.innerHTML = ""; drawBoard(); buildSteps(); counter.textContent = "Step 0 / " + steps.length; runBtn.textContent = "▶ Start"; }
// Writes one numbered line in the execution window, highlights it and scrolls down to it.
function log(text) { const prev = logBox.querySelector(".now"); if (prev) { prev.classList.remove("now"); } const d = document.createElement("div"); d.className = "now"; d.textContent = String(next).padStart(2, "0") + " │ " + text; logBox.appendChild(d); logBox.scrollTop = logBox.scrollHeight; }
// Runs the next step, writes its result, updates the counter, and stops by itself after the last step.
function stepOnce() { if (next >= steps.length) { pause(); return; } const text = steps[next](); next += 1; log(text); counter.textContent = "Step " + next + " / " + steps.length; if (next >= steps.length) { pause(); runBtn.textContent = "✓ Finished"; } }
// Starts (or resumes) the automatic run: one step now, then one step every DELAY milliseconds.
function start() { if (next >= steps.length) { return; } runBtn.textContent = "⏸ Pause"; stepOnce(); if (next < steps.length) { timer = setInterval(stepOnce, DELAY); } }
// Pauses the automatic run; the next Start continues from exactly the same step.
function pause() { clearInterval(timer); timer = null; if (next < steps.length) { runBtn.textContent = "▶ Start"; } }
// Copies SOURCE to the clipboard; if the browser blocks the Clipboard API (Application Programming Interface), a hidden text area is used instead.
function copyCode() { const b = document.getElementById("copy"); const done = function () { b.textContent = "✓ Copied"; setTimeout(function () { b.textContent = "⧉ Copy code"; }, 1500); }; const fallback = function () { const t = document.createElement("textarea"); t.value = SOURCE; document.body.appendChild(t); t.select(); document.execCommand("copy"); t.remove(); done(); }; if (navigator.clipboard && window.isSecureContext) { navigator.clipboard.writeText(SOURCE).then(done, fallback); } else { fallback(); } }
// Serializes the drawing as it is now into a self-contained SVG text (with the XML namespace and a white background).
function svgText() { const clone = svg.cloneNode(true); clone.setAttribute("xmlns", NS); const bg = document.createElementNS(NS, "rect"); bg.setAttribute("width", "100%"); bg.setAttribute("height", "100%"); bg.setAttribute("fill", "#FFFFFF"); clone.insertBefore(bg, clone.firstChild); return '<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>\n' + new XMLSerializer().serializeToString(clone); }
// Triggers a browser download of the given text or blob under the given file name.
function download(name, data, type) { const blob = data instanceof Blob ? data : new Blob([data], { type: type }); const url = URL.createObjectURL(blob); const a = document.createElement("a"); a.href = url; a.download = name; document.body.appendChild(a); a.click(); a.remove(); setTimeout(function () { URL.revokeObjectURL(url); }, 1000); }
// Download SVG button: saves the current drawing as a vector file.
document.getElementById("dlsvg").addEventListener("click", function () { download("ex1_kanban_board_pull.svg", svgText(), "image/svg+xml"); });
// Download PNG button: draws the current SVG on a hidden canvas at double resolution, then saves it as a picture file.
document.getElementById("dlpng").addEventListener("click", function () { const img = new Image(); const url = URL.createObjectURL(new Blob([svgText()], { type: "image/svg+xml" })); img.onload = function () { const c = document.createElement("canvas"); c.width = 760 * 2; c.height = 520 * 2; const g = c.getContext("2d"); g.fillStyle = "#FFFFFF"; g.fillRect(0, 0, c.width, c.height); g.drawImage(img, 0, 0, c.width, c.height); URL.revokeObjectURL(url); c.toBlob(function (b) { download("ex1_kanban_board_pull.png", b, "image/png"); }, "image/png"); }; img.src = url; });
// Start/Pause button: pauses if the program is running, otherwise starts or resumes it.
runBtn.addEventListener("click", function () { if (timer) { pause(); } else { start(); } });
// Next-step button: works only while paused, so the class sets the pace.
document.getElementById("stepBtn").addEventListener("click", function () { if (!timer) { stepOnce(); } });
// Restart button.
document.getElementById("reset").addEventListener("click", restart);
// Copy-code button.
document.getElementById("copy").addEventListener("click", copyCode);
// Draws the starting state as soon as the page is loaded.
restart();
// End of the program.
</script>
<!-- End of the visible page. -->
</body>
<!-- End of the document. -->
</html>

Step by step — what the program does

  1. Data first. DOW holds the six lines of the Definition of Workflow; COLUMNS holds the five states with their limit and their policy; CARDS holds the eight cards of October 26 with the column they start in and any date they already carry (story 4 is already In progress since Oct 15).
  2. The picture. drawBoard() draws one column per state with its name, its limit (≤ 2) and its policy in small text, the commitment point between Backlog and Ready and the delivery point before Done as two labelled vertical lines; drawCards() places every card in its column with its number, its points and its dates.
  3. One step per pull request. REQUESTS is the list of moves the team attempts, in order: each has a card, a target column and a day. The step calls tryPull(), which counts the cards already in the target column and compares the count with the limit.
  4. Performed or refused. When there is a free slot, the card moves, receives the date of the day (start date when entering In progress, finish date when entering Done) and the log says which clock started or stopped; when the column is full, the card does not move and the log prints the refusal and the policy that applies.
  5. Counts after every step. The last line of each log entry is the WIP count of every column — Ready, In progress, Review — so the class can see that the count never exceeds the limit.
  6. Controls. stepOnce() runs the step whose number is stored in next; Start calls it every 1.5 seconds; Pause stops the timer but keeps next, so Start resumes exactly where you stopped; Next step runs one step while paused; Restart rebuilds everything from zero; ⤓ SVG / ⤓ PNG save the board as it is now.
  7. Try it. In the copied code, change the limit of In progress from 2 to 3 and press Restart: Noah's spike is no longer refused on October 26 — and watch what that does to the number of cards that are finished by October 29.

Buttons: ▶ Start / ⏸ Pause (resumes where it stopped), ⏭ Next step, ↺ Restart, ⧉ Copy code, ⤓ SVG / ⤓ PNG (download the picture as it is now); every step is written in the execution window. A comment line precedes every line of code. Educational example, provided as is for your own study (Legal Notice, sections 4.2 and 11).

Flash-cards · Lesson 1 · click a card to flip it

Card 1.1 · question

What is a kanban in the Toyota Production System?

Answer

A visual card on a container of parts; when the parts are used, the card goes back to the preceding process as the order to make one more — nothing is produced until a card says something was used.

Card 1.2 · question

Pull versus push, in one sentence each?

Answer

Pull: the downstream process takes work when it has capacity and demand, and that is the signal to produce. Push: upstream hands work on when it is finished, whatever the capacity downstream.

Card 1.3 · question

Who carried Kanban into knowledge work, and when?

Answer

David J. Anderson: a pull system at Microsoft XIT in 2004, a card wall at Corbis in 2006–2007, the Kanban Method presented from 2007 and published as a book in 2010.

Card 1.4 · question

The six general practices of the Kanban Method (Kanban University)?

Answer

Visualize · limit WIP · manage flow · make policies explicit · implement feedback loops · improve collaboratively, evolve experimentally.

Card 1.5 · question

The six elements of a Definition of Workflow (Kanban Guide 2025.5)?

Answer

Work items · when an item is started and finished · the states between them · how WIP is controlled · explicit policies per state · a Service Level Expectation.

Card 1.6 · question

Commitment point and delivery point?

Answer

The commitment point is where the team decides it will do the item (entering Ready) — the lead-time clock starts; the delivery point is where the item is usable by the people it is for (entering Done) — the clock stops.

Self-check · Lesson 1

Formative · not counted toward grades

Four single-answer questions (MCQ) and two multiple-answer questions (MSQ — the number of correct options is given in round brackets). Choose, then reveal; every option has an explanation.

1. In the Toyota Production System, what makes the preceding process produce one more box of parts?MCQ · one correct answer
💡 Think of what travels backwards when a box is used.
2. Which statement about Kanban and roles, events and artifacts is correct?MCQ · one correct answer
💡 What does the Kanban Guide call itself?
3. On Team Menu's board the clock that measures how long a student waits for a promised story starts when a card…MCQ · one correct answer
💡 Where is the commitment point?
4. 'Review' written at the top of a column is a label. Which line turns it into an explicit policy of the Definition of Workflow?MCQ · one correct answer
💡 A policy says who, what and how many.
5. Which of these are elements that the Kanban Guide (2025.5) requires in a Definition of Workflow? (3)MSQ · 3 correct answers
💡 Six elements; three of these six options are among them.
6. Which statements describe a pull board rather than a push board? (2)MSQ · 2 correct answers
💡 Who decides that a card moves, and what is the signal?

Lesson 2 · WIP and WIP limits

0:17 – 0:27 · 10 minutes, then activity 0:27 – 0:32🎞 Slide 16

By the end of this lesson you can

  • Define WIP with the Kanban Guide's words — the number of work items started but not finished — and count it on a board.
  • Show with arithmetic, before any switching cost, why starting everything at once makes every item late and delays the first feedback.
  • Write a WIP limit as an explicit policy on a column, say what the team does when the column is full, and explain why the limit is a signal to talk and not a quota.

2.1 · What WIP is, and what it costs

🎞 Slide 17

The Kanban Guide defines WIP (Work In Progress) in nine words: "the number of work items started but not finished" (kanbanguides.org). It is a count of items — not of hours, not of points, not of people. On Team Menu's board on Thursday, October 15, the count was four: stories 1 and 3 started on October 12, story 2 on October 13, story 4 on October 15, and nothing finished. Four cards for four people looks like full employment. It is also four open promises, four pieces of work that nobody can use yet, and four reasons to switch from one thing to another.

Every started-but-unfinished item has a cost that a busy team does not see. It occupies attention even when nobody touches it — someone must remember where it stopped. It ages: the recipe cards it was based on change, the person who started it forgets the details, the test written for it drifts. And it delays feedback: the cafeteria manager cannot react to a French page that is 60 % done. The whole of this lesson follows from one observation: the number of things you work on at the same time is a decision, and most teams never make it on purpose.

2.2 · Why starting everything makes everything late

🎞 Slides 18–20

Take three stories of equal size, each needing three days of a team's full effort, all three committed on day 0. Policy A: start all three on day 0 and share the effort equally — one third of a day to each, every day. Policy B: start one, finish it, start the next.

Under policy A each story receives one third of the work per day, so each needs nine days: all three finish on day 9. Measured from the commitment on day 0, the three lead times are 9, 9 and 9 — an average of 9 days — and the first finished story appears on day 9. Under policy B the first story finishes on day 3, the second on day 6, the third on day 9: lead times of 3, 6 and 9, an average of 6 days, and the first finished story — the first feedback — on day 3. The total amount of work is identical, nine team-days; the last story finishes on the same day in both cases. What changes is the average lead time — a third shorter — and the date of the first delivery, three times earlier. Nothing in this arithmetic assumes that switching costs anything. It is pure queueing: when work shares a limited capacity, finishing one thing before starting the next shortens the average wait.

Switching does cost something as well, and the evidence is experimental rather than anecdotal. The APA (American Psychological Association) summarizes the work of Rubinstein, Meyer and Evans (2001, Journal of Experimental Psychology: Human Perception and Performance): changing task engages two control stages, goal shifting and rule activation, each costing a fraction of a second; the costs grow with the complexity and unfamiliarity of the tasks, and in some scenarios repeated switching was estimated to consume as much as 40 % of a person's productive time (apa.org). Activity 2 lets you measure a small version of it with a pen. Put the two effects together — the queueing arithmetic and the switching cost — and you have the reason behind the sentence the Kanban community has used since Arne Roock's 2012 booklet of that title: stop starting, start finishing.

2.3 · The WIP limit: a policy written on a column

🎞 Slide 21

A WIP limit is the fourth element of the DoW (Definition of Workflow) made concrete: a number written on a column — In progress ≤ 2 — that the team agrees not to exceed. It is an explicit policy, which means two things: everybody can read it, and changing it is a decision, not an accident. The Kanban Guide asks that the system "operate neither above nor below the agreed upon control": too high, and the arithmetic of 2.2 comes back; too low, and people wait for a slot while they could help. The pull rule of Lesson 1 is the direct consequence of the limit — the Guide says that controlling WIP (Work In Progress) "should create a pull system" — because a full column is precisely the absence of the signal to start.

Where does the number come from? Atlassian's guidance for a first limit is observation: count how many items each state actually holds over a few weeks, choose a number as a team, and resist changing it for a while so that the effect can be seen (Atlassian, WIP limits). A practical starting point for a small team is a limit below the number of people — three people, limit two — so that at least one person is always free to finish rather than start. The limit may apply to one column, to several, or to the whole board from the commitment point to the delivery point.

What happens when the column is full is the part teams get wrong. The limit is not a reason to stand idle, and it is not a punishment for the person whose card is slow. A full column is a signal to finish: pair with the person on the oldest card, take the card that waits in Review, remove the blocker, or — if none of those is possible — improve the policy. Dan Radigan's phrase for it is that limits make blockers and bottlenecks visible, so that the team can swarm on them (Atlassian). A limit that is never reached is too high to teach anything; a limit that is reached and respected is where the conversation about flow begins.

2.4 · Team Menu's limit, written down

🎞 Slide 22

In its Sprint 1 Retrospective Team Menu wrote: "Amira owns a limit of two stories In progress at once, checked at each Daily Scrum from October 26." That sentence is already a policy in all but form: a number (two), a scope (the In progress column), a moment of inspection (the Daily Scrum) and an owner of the count (Amira — who counts, not who decides alone). Written at the top of the column, with the second limit on Review (one card, because the second-person check is one shared step), it becomes the board of Lesson 1 and the first line of today's studio. Activity 2 is the two-minute experience of why that line was worth writing.

Terms to learn

WIP (Work In Progress)
The number of work items started but not finished (Kanban Guide) — a count of items, not of hours, points or people.
Cost of WIP
What every started-but-unfinished item consumes: attention, ageing of the information it was based on, and delayed feedback for the people who wait for it.
Average lead time under shared capacity
Three equal stories, three days each: start all at once → lead times 9, 9, 9 (average 9); one at a time → 3, 6, 9 (average 6), same total work, first delivery three times earlier.
Switching cost
The time and accuracy lost each time a person changes task (goal shifting and rule activation — Rubinstein, Meyer & Evans, 2001, summarized by the APA); it grows with the complexity of the tasks.
Stop starting, start finishing
The Kanban community's sentence for the two effects above (title of Arne Roock's 2012 booklet): with limited capacity, finishing before starting shortens the average wait.
WIP limit
A number written on a column — or on the whole board between the commitment point and the delivery point — that the team agrees not to exceed; an explicit policy, changed only by decision.
Neither above nor below
The Kanban Guide's rule for the limit: above it, the queueing cost returns; below it, people wait for a slot while they could help finish.
First limit
Atlassian's advice: observe how many items each state really holds, choose as a team, keep it long enough to see the effect; for a small team, a limit below the number of people.
Full column
The signal to finish rather than start: pair on the oldest card, take the waiting Review, remove the blocker, or improve the policy — never idle, never a punishment.
Swarming
Several members working on one item to finish it, the usual answer to a full column.
Owner of the count
The member who checks the WIP count at each Daily Scrum (Team Menu: Amira); the decision to change the limit remains the team's.

Activity 2 · Mini-exercise — the multitasking demo · 0:27 – 0:32 · 5 min

🎞 Slide 23

Pen and paper, in pairs; one writes, one times with the phone. Three names of the same length — for example KANBAN, TOYOTA, REVIEW (six letters each).

  1. Round 1, interleaved (the four-cards-at-once team): write the first letter of name 1, then the first letter of name 2, then of name 3, then the second letter of name 1, and so on, until all three names are complete. Time it. Count the mistakes.
  2. Round 2, one at a time (the limit-of-one team): write name 1 completely, then name 2, then name 3. Time it. Count the mistakes.
  3. Swap roles and repeat if time allows. Then compute, on paper: time of round 1 ÷ time of round 2, and the moment the first name was finished in each round.

One minute at the end: two pairs report their ratio. The work was identical — eighteen letters — in both rounds.

Real-life example 2 · Team Menu replays its Sprint 1 under three WIP policies — a model with stated assumptions

🎞 Slides 19–20
The task

Team Menu takes the four stories of its Sprint 1 — 1 (3 points), 2 (1), 3 (2) and 4 (3), nine points in all — and asks what would have happened to the finish dates under three policies: start everything at once (what the team actually did, WIP (Work In Progress) 4), a limit of two, and a limit of one. It is a model, built on three stated assumptions, and the team writes those assumptions before the numbers, as Lab 04 will ask: one point of a story needs one day of the team's whole shared effort; when several stories are in progress, the day's effort is split equally among them; the stories are taken smallest first when a slot opens. A fourth, optional assumption — a switching cost of 20 % of the day's effort for every story in progress beyond the first — is kept at zero in the first run and switched on in the second.

Relation to the lecture

It is section 2.2 computed on real cards instead of three identical boxes — the average lead time and the date of the first finished story under each policy — and section 2.3 applied: what a limit of two would have changed, which is the policy Team Menu wrote in its Retrospective and the one today's studio asks every team to write on its board.

Run 1 — no switching cost (the clean queueing effect). Effort units per day: 1. Commitment of all four stories: day 0.

Policy What happens day by day Finish days (stories 2, 3, 1, 4) Average lead time First story finished
WIP 4 — start all four, equal split 0.25 per story per day; story 2 (1 pt) is done at day 4; then three stories share, story 3 (1 pt left) finishes at day 7; then stories 1 and 4 (1 pt left each) share and finish together at day 9 4 · 7 · 9 · 9 7.25 days day 4
WIP 2 — two at a time, smallest first stories 2 and 3 share (0.5 each): 2 is done at day 2, 3 at day 4; story 1 starts on day 3 (0.5 per day), story 4 on day 5; 1 is done at day 8, 4 at day 9 2 · 4 · 8 · 9 5.75 days day 2
WIP 1 — one at a time, smallest first 2 → 3 → 1 → 4, each at full effort 1 · 3 · 6 · 9 4.75 days day 1

Read the table from right to left. The last story finishes on day 9 under every policy — the total work is nine points and the team has one unit per day; no policy changes that. The first finished story moves from day 4 to day 1, and the average lead time falls from 7.25 to 4.75 days. That is the effect of section 2.2 with Team Menu's own sizes: the smaller stories stop waiting behind the larger ones.

Run 2 — the same three policies with a switching cost of 20 % per extra story in progress. With four stories in progress the day's useful effort falls to 1 − 3 × 0.2 = 0.4 units, a tenth of a point per story per day; with two stories, to 0.8; with one, it stays at 1.0. Now the policies no longer finish on the same day: under WIP 4 the first story is finished on day 10 and the last on day 18 (finish days 10 · 15 · 18 · 18, average lead time 15.25 days); under WIP 2, days 3 · 5 · 11 · 12 (average 7.75, last on day 12); under WIP 1 nothing changes — 1 · 3 · 6 · 9 — because one story in progress has nothing to switch to. The switching cost is an assumption, and the team says so; the direction of the result does not depend on its exact size, only the distance between the policies does.

What Team Menu wrote under the table (the three lines Lab 04 asks for). Assumptions: one point = one team-day; equal split; smallest first; switching cost 0 % in run 1, 20 % in run 2. Result: in the model, a limit of two cuts our average lead time from 7.25 to 5.75 days (run 1) and gives the cafeteria manager a finished story on day 2 instead of day 4; with switching counted, the gap widens to 15.25 against 7.75. Decision: In progress ≤ 2 from October 26, checked by Amira at each Daily Scrum.

Where this goes next. The limit is the policy on today's studio board; the model is Example 2, which you can run with your own stories by changing one list; Part C of the Mid-Term (November 16) asks you to recommend a WIP (Work In Progress) limit for a given table and to justify it — this is the justification.

Team Menu, its members and its data are fictional. Your own board and tables must contain no personal information about anyone outside your team (Legal Notice, section 20).

Code example 2 · WIP policy simulator — start everything, or stop starting

🎞 Slide 24
The task

Simulates Team Menu's four Sprint 1 stories day by day under three policies — WIP 4 (start everything), WIP 2 and WIP 1 — with one unit of team effort per day split equally among the stories in progress and the smallest story taken first when a slot opens. For each policy it draws the progress bars of the four stories, marks each finish day, and computes the average lead time and the day of the first finished story. A second run adds a switching cost of 20 % per extra story in progress and shows how the totals move.

Relation to the lecture

It is the arithmetic of section 2.2 (shared capacity, average lead time, first delivery) and the table of this lesson's real-life example, step by step; the limit it demonstrates is the policy of section 2.3.

Printed copy: the picture shows the example after its last step. The interactive version (buttons, step-by-step log, downloads) is in the HTML page and in 01_code/ex2_wip_policy_simulator.html of the companion ZIP.

For each policy it draws the four progress bars, marks every finish day on a timeline, and computes the average lead time and the day of the first finished story; a second run adds a switching cost of 20 % per extra story in progress. <script>
// Strict mode: JavaScript reports silent mistakes (for example an undeclared variable) as errors.
"use strict";
// Keeps a copy of this page's source now, before the program changes anything, for the Copy button.
const SOURCE = "<!DOCTYPE html>\n" + document.documentElement.outerHTML;
// The SVG (Scalable Vector Graphics) namespace: every drawing element has to be created in it.
const NS = "http://www.w3.org/2000/svg";
// Shortcut to the drawing surface.
const svg = document.getElementById("viz");
// Shortcut to the execution window.
const logBox = document.getElementById("log");
// Shortcut to the Start/Pause button.
const runBtn = document.getElementById("run");
// Shortcut to the step counter.
const counter = document.getElementById("counter");
// Index of the next step to run (0 means that nothing has run yet).
let next = 0;
// Handle of the repeating timer while the program runs; null while it is paused.
let timer = null;
// The ordered list of steps; each step is a function that does one action and returns the text for the log.
const steps = [];
// Creates one SVG element with the given attributes, attaches it to a parent (default: the drawing) and returns it.
function el(tag, attrs, parent) { const e = document.createElementNS(NS, tag); for (const k in attrs) { e.setAttribute(k, attrs[k]); } (parent || svg).appendChild(e); return e; }
// Writes text at (x, y); the options set size, weight, colour, alignment and parent.
function txt(x, y, s, o) { o = o || {}; const t = el("text", { x: x, y: y, "font-size": o.size || 12, "font-weight": o.weight || 400, fill: o.fill || C.ink, "text-anchor": o.anchor || "start", "font-family": "system-ui, Segoe UI, Roboto, Arial, sans-serif" }, o.parent); t.textContent = s; return t; }
// Splits a sentence into lines of at most max characters, so that it fits inside a box.
function wrap(s, max) { const out = []; let line = ""; for (const w of s.split(" ")) { if ((line + " " + w).trim().length > max) { out.push(line.trim()); line = w; } else { line += " " + w; } } out.push(line.trim()); return out; }
// Brand colours used by the drawing: teal, indigo and rust (a colour-blind-safe set) plus neutral inks.
const C = { teal: "#0A918E", indigo: "#4A3AA7", rust: "#B5440C", ink: "#1B2B2E", muted: "#54646A", line: "#DDD3C4", soft: "#F6F3EE", grid: "#E7E1D6", tealT: "#E4F3F2", indigoT: "#ECEAF7", rustT: "#FBEFE8" };
// Pause between two automatic steps, in milliseconds (short, because one step is one simulated day).
const DELAY = 900;
// INPUT 1 — the four Sprint 1 stories of Team Menu: id, short title and size in points (one point = one team-day of effort).
const STORIES = [
// Story 2, the smallest: the allergen shown on every dish.
{ id: "2", title: "sesame shown on every dish", pts: 1 },
// Story 3: an icon next to each allergen.
{ id: "3", title: "an icon next to each allergen", pts: 2 },
// Story 1: today's three hot meals.
{ id: "1", title: "today's three hot meals", pts: 3 },
// Story 4: the page in French.
{ id: "4", title: "the page in French", pts: 3 }
// End of the stories (nine points in all).
];
// INPUT 2 — the three WIP limits to compare, in the order they are run.
const POLICIES = [4, 2, 1];
// INPUT 3 — the two runs: the switching cost per extra story in progress (0 in run 1, 0.2 = 20 % in run 2).
const RUNS = [0, 0.2];
// INPUT 4 — the team's shared effort per day, in points (one unit).
const DAY_EFFORT = 1.0;
// The smallest useful effort a day can keep, so that a very high switching cost never stops the work completely.
const MIN_EFFORT = 0.1;
// The number of pixels one simulated day takes on a panel's timeline (18 days fit in a panel).
const DAY_PX = 11.5;
// Simulates one policy from day 1 until every story is finished; returns one record per day (a pure function: no drawing).
function runPolicy(limit, switchCost) {
// Working copies of the stories: remaining effort, start day and finish day.
const st = STORIES.map(function (s) { return { id: s.id, pts: s.pts, rem: s.pts, start: null, done: null }; });
// The day records returned to the caller.
const records = [];
// Day counter and count of finished stories.
let day = 0, finished = 0;
// One loop turn = one day; the cap of 60 days protects against an endless loop if the inputs are changed badly.
while (finished < st.length && day < 60) {
// A new day begins.
day += 1;
// Stories in progress at the start of the day: started and not finished.
const inprog = st.filter(function (s) { return s.start !== null && s.done === null; });
// Stories still waiting, smallest remaining effort first (ties: lower id first).
const waiting = st.filter(function (s) { return s.start === null; }).sort(function (a, b) { return a.rem - b.rem || (a.id < b.id ? -1 : 1); });
// The ids pulled this morning, for the log.
const pulled = [];
// The pull rule: fill the free slots under the limit from the waiting list.
while (inprog.length < limit && waiting.length) { const s = waiting.shift(); s.start = day; inprog.push(s); pulled.push(s.id); }
// Number of stories in progress today.
const n = inprog.length;
// Useful effort of the day: the whole unit minus the switching cost for every story beyond the first, never below the minimum.
const eff = Math.max(MIN_EFFORT, DAY_EFFORT - switchCost * (n - 1));
// Equal split of the useful effort among the stories in progress.
const share = eff / n;
// Every story in progress receives its share.
inprog.forEach(function (s) { s.rem -= share; });
// Stories whose remaining effort reached zero (a tiny tolerance absorbs floating-point rounding) are finished today.
const doneToday = [];
// Marks the finished stories and counts them.
inprog.forEach(function (s) { if (s.rem <= 1e-9 && s.done === null) { s.rem = 0; s.done = day; finished += 1; doneToday.push(s.id); } });
// Stores the day's record: a snapshot of every story plus the day's numbers.
records.push({ day: day, pulled: pulled, n: n, eff: eff, share: share, finished: doneToday, snap: st.map(function (s) { return { id: s.id, pts: s.pts, rem: s.rem, start: s.start, done: s.done }; }) });
// End of the day loop.
}
// Returns the records of all days.
return records;
// End of runPolicy.
}
// Computes the summary numbers of a finished policy from its last record: finish days, average lead time, first finish.
function summary(records) { const last = records[records.length - 1].snap; const days = last.map(function (s) { return s.done; }); const avg = days.reduce(function (a, b) { return a + b; }, 0) / days.length; const first = Math.min.apply(null, days); return { days: days, avg: avg, first: first, lastDay: Math.max.apply(null, days) }; }

RUNS.forEach(function (sw, r) { POLICIES.forEach(function (limit, c) {
// Panel background.
const x = panelX(c), y = panelY(r);

const ax = x + 12, ay = y + 152;

el("line", { x1: ax, y1: ay, x2: ax + 18 * DAY_PX, y2: ay, stroke: C.muted });

for (let d = 0; d <= 18; d += 3) { el("line", { x1: ax + d * DAY_PX, y1: ay, x2: ax + d * DAY_PX, y2: ay + 4, stroke: C.muted }); txt(ax + d * DAY_PX, ay + 14, String(d), { size: 8, fill: C.muted, anchor: "middle" }); }
// Axis caption.
txt(ax, ay + 26, "finish days (= lead times; all stories committed on day 0)", { size: 8, fill: C.muted });
// Two result lines, filled when the policy runs.
const avgT = txt(x + 8, y + 196, "average lead time: —", { size: 10, weight: 700 });
// The first-finish line.
const firstT = txt(x + 8, y + 212, "first story finished: —  ·  last: —", { size: 9.5, fill: C.muted });
// A day counter in the top-right corner.
const dayT = txt(x + 228, y + 16, "", { size: 9.5, weight: 700, fill: C.rust, anchor: "end" });
// The layer for the moving parts (bar fills, finish dots).
const layer = el("g", {});
// Stores the parts.
panels[r + "-" + c] = { frame: frame, avgT: avgT, firstT: firstT, dayT: dayT, layer: layer, x: x, y: y, ax: ax, ay: ay };
// End of the loops over policies and runs.
}); });
// End of drawFrame.
}
// Redraws one panel from a day record: the filled part of each bar, the finish dots on the timeline and the running numbers.
function drawDay(r, c, rec, limit) { const p = panels[r + "-" + c]; p.layer.innerHTML = ""; p.dayT.textContent = "day " + rec.day; Object.keys(panels).forEach(function (k) { panels[k].frame.setAttribute("stroke", C.line); panels[k].frame.setAttribute("stroke-width", 1); }); p.frame.setAttribute("stroke", C.teal); p.frame.setAttribute("stroke-width", 2); rec.snap.forEach(function (s, i) { const ry = p.y + 28 + i * 24; const doneW = (s.pts - s.rem) * 40; if (doneW > 0) { el("rect", { x: p.x + 56, y: ry + 3, width: doneW, height: 13, rx: 3, fill: s.done ? C.teal : (s.start ? C.indigo : "#fff") }, p.layer); } if (s.start && !s.done) { txt(p.x + 56 + s.pts * 40 + 5, ry + 13, s.rem.toFixed(1) + " left", { size: 8.5, fill: C.indigo, parent: p.layer }); } if (s.done) { txt(p.x + 56 + s.pts * 40 + 5, ry + 13, "done day " + s.done, { size: 8.5, weight: 700, fill: C.teal, parent: p.layer }); el("circle", { cx: p.ax + s.done * DAY_PX, cy: p.ay - 1 - (i % 2) * 7, r: 3.5, fill: C.teal, stroke: "#fff" }, p.layer); txt(p.ax + s.done * DAY_PX, p.ay - 12 - (i % 2) * 7, "#" + s.id, { size: 7.5, fill: C.teal, anchor: "middle", parent: p.layer }); } }); const done = rec.snap.filter(function (s) { return s.done; }); if (done.length) { const avg = done.reduce(function (a, s) { return a + s.done; }, 0) / done.length; p.avgT.textContent = "average lead time: " + avg.toFixed(2) + " d (" + done.length + " of 4 finished)"; p.firstT.textContent = "first story finished: day " + Math.min.apply(null, done.map(function (s) { return s.done; })) + (done.length === 4 ? "  ·  last: day " + Math.max.apply(null, done.map(function (s) { return s.done; })) : "  ·  last: —"); } }
// Builds the ordered list of steps from the simulation records.
function buildSteps() {
// Empties the list (needed by Restart).
steps.length = 0;
// Step 1: what the program will do.
steps.push(function () { return "Start · six simulations: WIP 4, 2 and 1, first without a switching cost (run 1), then with 20 % per extra story (run 2). One step = one simulated day."; });
// Step 2: the inputs and the three assumptions.
steps.push(function () { return "Inputs · stories #2 (1 pt), #3 (2), #1 (3), #4 (3) = 9 points; all committed on day 0. Assumptions: one point = one team-day; the day's effort (1.0) is split equally among the stories in progress; the smallest remaining story is pulled first when a slot opens; useful effort = 1.0 − switching cost × (stories in progress − 1), never below 0.1."; });
// The results of every policy, filled as the runs are generated.
const results = [];
// One block of steps per run and policy.
RUNS.forEach(function (sw, r) { POLICIES.forEach(function (limit, c) {
// Runs the simulation once, now, so that each day step only has to draw a record.
const records = runPolicy(limit, sw);
// The summary of this policy.
const sum = summary(records);
// Keeps it for the final table.
results.push({ run: r + 1, sw: sw, limit: limit, sum: sum });
// A header step for the policy.
steps.push(function () { return "— Run " + (r + 1) + " · WIP ≤ " + limit + " · switching cost " + Math.round(sw * 100) + " % —  prediction time: how many days until the first finished story, and what average?"; });
// One step per simulated day.
records.forEach(function (rec) { steps.push(function () { drawDay(r, c, rec, limit); const names = rec.snap.filter(function (s) { return s.start && (s.done === null || rec.finished.indexOf(s.id) >= 0); }).map(function (s) { return "#" + s.id; }).join(" "); const rems = rec.snap.filter(function (s) { return s.start !== null; }).map(function (s) { return "#" + s.id + " " + s.rem.toFixed(2); }).join(" · "); return "Run " + (r + 1) + " · WIP " + limit + " · day " + rec.day + (rec.pulled.length ? " · pulled: #" + rec.pulled.join(" #") : "") + " · in progress: " + names + " (" + rec.n + ") · useful effort " + rec.eff.toFixed(2) + " → " + rec.share.toFixed(2) + " each · remaining: " + rems + (rec.finished.length ? "\n     FINISHED: #" + rec.finished.join(", #") + " on day " + rec.day + " (lead time " + rec.day + " days, committed day 0)" : ""); }); });
// A closing step for the policy with its numbers.
steps.push(function () { return "Result · run " + (r + 1) + " · WIP ≤ " + limit + " · finish days (stories 2, 3, 1, 4): " + sum.days.join(" · ") + " · average lead time " + sum.avg.toFixed(2) + " days · first finished story on day " + sum.first + " · last on day " + sum.lastDay + "."; });
// End of the loops.
}); });
// Last step: the comparison table.
steps.push(function () { const lines = results.map(function (x) { return "run " + x.run + " · WIP " + x.limit + " · switch " + Math.round(x.sw * 100) + " %  → " + x.sum.days.join("·") + "  avg " + x.sum.avg.toFixed(2) + " d  first day " + x.sum.first + "  last day " + x.sum.lastDay; }); return "Done · comparison:\n     " + lines.join("\n     ") + "\n     Reading: in run 1 the last story finishes on day 9 under every policy (nine points, one unit per day — no policy changes that), but the first finished story moves from day 4 to day 1 and the average lead time from 7.25 to 4.75 days. In run 2 the policies no longer finish on the same day: switching has a price, and the limit avoids paying it. The ranking of the policies does not depend on the size of the switching cost; only the distance between them does. Team Menu's decision: In progress ≤ 2 from October 26."; });
// End of buildSteps.
}
// Restart: stops, clears the log, redraws the empty frame, rebuilds the steps and returns to step 0.
function restart() { pause(); next = 0; panels = {}; logBox.innerHTML = ""; drawFrame(); buildSteps(); counter.textContent = "Step 0 / " + steps.length; runBtn.textContent = "▶ Start"; }
// Writes one numbered line in the execution window, highlights it and scrolls down to it.
function log(text) { const prev = logBox.querySelector(".now"); if (prev) { prev.classList.remove("now"); } const d = document.createElement("div"); d.className = "now"; d.textContent = String(next).padStart(2, "0") + " │ " + text; logBox.appendChild(d); logBox.scrollTop = logBox.scrollHeight; }
// Runs the next step, writes its result, updates the counter, and stops by itself after the last step.
function stepOnce() { if (next >= steps.length) { pause(); return; } const text = steps[next](); next += 1; log(text); counter.textContent = "Step " + next + " / " + steps.length; if (next >= steps.length) { pause(); runBtn.textContent = "✓ Finished"; } }
// Starts (or resumes) the automatic run: one step now, then one step every DELAY milliseconds.
function start() { if (next >= steps.length) { return; } runBtn.textContent = "⏸ Pause"; stepOnce(); if (next < steps.length) { timer = setInterval(stepOnce, DELAY); } }
// Pauses the automatic run; the next Start continues from exactly the same step.
function pause() { clearInterval(timer); timer = null; if (next < steps.length) { runBtn.textContent = "▶ Start"; } }
// Copies SOURCE to the clipboard; if the browser blocks the Clipboard API (Application Programming Interface), a hidden text area is used instead.
function copyCode() { const b = document.getElementById("copy"); const done = function () { b.textContent = "✓ Copied"; setTimeout(function () { b.textContent = "⧉ Copy code"; }, 1500); }; const fallback = function () { const t = document.createElement("textarea"); t.value = SOURCE; document.body.appendChild(t); t.select(); document.execCommand("copy"); t.remove(); done(); }; if (navigator.clipboard && window.isSecureContext) { navigator.clipboard.writeText(SOURCE).then(done, fallback); } else { fallback(); } }
// Serializes the drawing as it is now into a self-contained SVG text (with the XML namespace and a white background).
function svgText() { const clone = svg.cloneNode(true); clone.setAttribute("xmlns", NS); const bg = document.createElementNS(NS, "rect"); bg.setAttribute("width", "100%"); bg.setAttribute("height", "100%"); bg.setAttribute("fill", "#FFFFFF"); clone.insertBefore(bg, clone.firstChild); return '<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>\n' + new XMLSerializer().serializeToString(clone); }
// Triggers a browser download of the given text or blob under the given file name.
function download(name, data, type) { const blob = data instanceof Blob ? data : new Blob([data], { type: type }); const url = URL.createObjectURL(blob); const a = document.createElement("a"); a.href = url; a.download = name; document.body.appendChild(a); a.click(); a.remove(); setTimeout(function () { URL.revokeObjectURL(url); }, 1000); }
// Download SVG button: saves the current drawing as a vector file.
document.getElementById("dlsvg").addEventListener("click", function () { download("ex2_wip_policy_simulator.svg", svgText(), "image/svg+xml"); });
// Download PNG button: draws the current SVG on a hidden canvas at double resolution, then saves it as a picture file.
document.getElementById("dlpng").addEventListener("click", function () { const img = new Image(); const url = URL.createObjectURL(new Blob([svgText()], { type: "image/svg+xml" })); img.onload = function () { const c = document.createElement("canvas"); c.width = 760 * 2; c.height = 520 * 2; const g = c.getContext("2d"); g.fillStyle = "#FFFFFF"; g.fillRect(0, 0, c.width, c.height); g.drawImage(img, 0, 0, c.width, c.height); URL.revokeObjectURL(url); c.toBlob(function (b) { download("ex2_wip_policy_simulator.png", b, "image/png"); }, "image/png"); }; img.src = url; });
// Start/Pause button: pauses if the program is running, otherwise starts or resumes it.
runBtn.addEventListener("click", function () { if (timer) { pause(); } else { start(); } });
// Next-step button: works only while paused, so the class sets the pace.
document.getElementById("stepBtn").addEventListener("click", function () { if (!timer) { stepOnce(); } });
// Restart button.
document.getElementById("reset").addEventListener("click", restart);
// Copy-code button.
document.getElementById("copy").addEventListener("click", copyCode);
// Draws the starting state as soon as the page is loaded.
restart();
// End of the program.
</script>
<!-- End of the visible page. -->
</body>

Step by step — what the program does

  1. Inputs. STORIES holds the four stories with their points (the effort in team-days); POLICIES holds the three limits to compare; SWITCH_COST is 0 for the first run and 0.2 for the second; DAY_EFFORT is the team's shared effort per day, 1.0.
  2. One day per step. For the current policy, simulateDay() first pulls stories into progress while the count is under the limit (smallest remaining first), then computes the useful effort of the day — DAY_EFFORT − SWITCH_COST × (in progress − 1), never below 0.1 — and splits it equally among the stories in progress.
  3. Finishing. When a story's remaining effort reaches zero it is marked finished on that day; the day is its lead time, because every story was committed on day 0. The log prints who received what and who finished.
  4. The picture. One panel per policy: four horizontal bars (remaining effort shrinks from the right), a dot on the finish day, and two numbers that update as the run proceeds — average lead time of the finished stories and the day of the first finish.
  5. Switching the policy. When a policy is complete, the next step resets the stories and continues with the next limit; after the three limits of run 1, the switching cost is set to 0.2 and the three policies run again in the second row of panels.
  6. Controls. Start / Pause / Next step / Restart / Copy / ⤓ SVG / ⤓ PNG, as in Example 1. Pause at the end of each policy and ask the class to predict the average of the next one before pressing Next step.
  7. Try it. In the copied code, replace the four stories by your own Sprint 1 stories and their points, press Restart, and read your own three averages; then set SWITCH_COST to 0.1 and see that the ranking of the policies does not change.

Buttons: ▶ Start / ⏸ Pause (resumes where it stopped), ⏭ Next step, ↺ Restart, ⧉ Copy code, ⤓ SVG / ⤓ PNG (download the picture as it is now); every step is written in the execution window. A comment line precedes every line of code. Educational example, provided as is for your own study (Legal Notice, sections 4.2 and 11).

Flash-cards · Lesson 2 · click a card to flip it

Card 2.1 · question

Definition of WIP (Kanban Guide)?

Answer

The number of work items started but not finished — a count of items, not of hours, points or people.

Card 2.2 · question

Three equal stories of three days, all committed on day 0: lead times if all are started at once, and if one is started at a time?

Answer

All at once: 9, 9, 9 (average 9, first finish on day 9). One at a time: 3, 6, 9 (average 6, first finish on day 3). Same total work.

Card 2.3 · question

What does switching tasks cost, according to the APA summary of Rubinstein, Meyer and Evans (2001)?

Answer

Two control stages — goal shifting and rule activation — each costing time; the costs add up with every switch, grow with complexity, and were estimated at up to 40 % of productive time in some scenarios.

Card 2.4 · question

What is a WIP limit?

Answer

A number written on a column (or on the whole board between the commitment and delivery points) that the team agrees not to exceed — an explicit policy, changed only by decision.

Card 2.5 · question

The column is full. What does the team do?

Answer

Finish rather than start: pair on the oldest card, take the card waiting in Review, remove the blocker, or improve the policy; never stand idle, never treat it as a punishment.

Card 2.6 · question

How does a team choose a first WIP limit?

Answer

Observe how many items each state really holds, decide as a team, keep the number long enough to see the effect; for a small team, a limit below the number of people.
