Lesson 3 · Lead time, cycle time, throughput, Little's Law

0:32 – 0:42 · 10 minutes, then activity 0:42 – 0:47🎞 Slide 25

By the end of this lesson you can

  • Compute lead time, cycle time and work item age from the three dates on a card, in elapsed calendar days, and always answer the question 'from when?'.
  • Compute throughput as a count of finished items per unit of time, and tell it apart from velocity.
  • Apply Little's Law — average cycle time = average WIP ÷ throughput — to a clean example and to your own data, and name the conditions under which it holds.

3.1 · Three clocks on one card

🎞 Slides 26–27

Every card on the board of Lesson 1 carries three dates, and from three dates you can compute three durations. The Kanban Guide defines two of them in elapsed time. Cycle time is "the elapsed time between when a work item started and when a work item finished" — from the day the card entered In progress to the day it entered Done. Work item age is "the elapsed time between when a work item started and the current date" — the same clock, read before the card has finished (kanbanguides.org). The third duration starts earlier. Lead time, in the Kanban University vocabulary and in this course, is the elapsed time from the commitment point — the day the card entered Ready — to the delivery point; Atlassian's board article says the same thing in one line: the time between the commitment point and the delivery point is called lead time (atlassian.com). Lead time is the clock the student who was promised the French page experiences; cycle time is the clock the team controls most directly; age is the clock that tells you, today, which card to help.

Two rules make these numbers comparable between teams and between weeks. First, they are elapsed durations — calendar days, including days when nobody touched the card — because the people who wait experience calendar time, not effort; Daniel Vacanti makes this point explicitly in the ProKanban pocket guide (prokanban.org). Second, a team writes its counting convention in its Definition of Workflow. This course counts the difference between the two dates: a card started on Monday and finished on Friday has a cycle time of 4 days (Friday minus Monday). Some teams count both ends and say 5; neither is wrong, but a team that has not written which one it uses will argue about it in every Review. Whenever a number is given, the first question is therefore "from when?" — and the second is "counted how?".

Team Menu's four Sprint 1 cards, with the convention above: story 2 was committed on October 12, started on the 13th and finished on the 16th — lead time 4 days, cycle time 3; story 1, started on the 12th and finished on the 19th — 7 and 7; story 3, started on the 12th and finished on the 22nd — 10 and 10, of which about five days were waiting after the Daily Scrum of the 17th decided that the icons would wait for the French page; story 4, started on the 15th and not finished by the 25th — no lead time yet, no cycle time yet, and an age of 10 days on October 25, 11 on the morning of this class.

3.2 · Throughput — counting what comes out

🎞 Slide 29

Throughput is "the number of work items finished per unit of time", and the Guide adds that the measurement is "the exact count of work items" (kanbanguides.org). Three things follow. The unit is an item, not a point: a finished one-point story and a finished five-point story each count as one. The period is the team's choice and must be stated — per day, per week, per Sprint. And throughput is not velocity: velocity (Class 5) sums the story points of the stories that met the Definition of Done in a Sprint; throughput counts the stories. The two measure different things and are used for different forecasts: velocity for "how many points can we plan", throughput for "how many cards will come out next week".

Team Menu finished three stories in the 14 days of Sprint 1: a throughput of 3 ÷ 14 ≈ 0.21 items per day, or 1.5 items per week. Per week the count was uneven — one story in the week of October 12 (story 2, on the 16th), two in the week of October 19 (stories 1 and 3) — which is normal for four cards and the reason flow metrics are read over longer periods than one Sprint.

3.3 · Little's Law

🎞 Slide 30

In 1961 John D. C. Little proved a relation that holds for any queue in a stable state: L = λW — the average number of items in a system (L) equals the average rate at which items arrive (λ, the Greek letter lambda) multiplied by the average time an item spends in the system (W) (Operations Research, 1961). In a stable system items leave at the same average rate as they arrive, so the arrival rate can be replaced by the throughput, and the law reads, in the vocabulary of this lesson:

average WIP = throughput × average cycle time, or, rearranged, average cycle time = average WIP ÷ throughput.

The class example: a team keeps on average 8 items in progress and finishes 2 items per day; its average cycle time is 8 ÷ 2 = 4 days. The units must match: WIP (Work In Progress) in items, throughput in items per day, cycle time in days. If the throughput is given per week, the cycle time comes out in weeks — 15 items in progress and 5 finished per week give 3 weeks, not 3 days.

The law is exact only under conditions, and Daniel Vacanti lists five for the flow version in Actionable Agile Metrics for Predictability (2015): the average arrival rate equals the average departure rate; every item that enters the system eventually leaves it; the WIP (Work In Progress) at the start and at the end of the period is about the same; the average age of the items in progress is neither growing nor shrinking; and all quantities use consistent units. None of these is exotic — together they say "a stable system, measured over long enough" — and the practical consequence is the one that matters for your board: at the same throughput, less WIP means shorter cycle times. Lowering the limit of Lesson 2 does not make the team work faster; it makes each item wait less, which is what the people waiting experience.

3.4 · Team Menu's check, and why it does not match

🎞 Slide 31

Team Menu computes the law on its own fourteen days. The daily count of cards in progress — 2, 3, 3, 4, 3, 3, 3, 2, 2, 2, 1, 1, 1, 1 — sums to 31; the average WIP is 31 ÷ 14 ≈ 2.2 items. The throughput is 0.21 items per day. The law predicts an average cycle time of 2.2 ÷ 0.21 ≈ 10.3 days; the three finished stories show (3 + 7 + 10) ÷ 3 ≈ 6.7 days. The two numbers do not agree, and that is the result to write down, not to hide: the conditions are not met. The window opened with zero cards and closed with one; story 4 entered and never left; the whole sample is four cards. Lab 04 asks for exactly this — one Little's Law line with the predicted number, the observed number and one sentence on the gap — because a team that can explain why its numbers disagree understands the law better than a team whose numbers happened to agree. Activity 3 gives you three clean cases first.

Terms to learn

Cycle time
The elapsed time between when a work item started (entered In progress) and when it finished (entered Done) — Kanban Guide; in this course the difference of the two dates, in calendar days.
Work item age
The elapsed time between when a work item started and the current date — the cycle-time clock read before the item has finished; the number that says which card to help today.
Lead time
The elapsed time from the commitment point (the card entered Ready) to the delivery point (Done) — Kanban University vocabulary; the clock the person who was promised the item experiences.
Elapsed time
Calendar time including the days nobody touched the card, because the people who wait experience calendar time; never 'active hours'.
Counting convention
The rule written in the Definition of Workflow for turning two dates into days; this course: finish date minus start date (Monday → Friday = 4 days).
From when?
The question to ask before accepting any flow number: which point starts the clock — commitment, start, or now.
Throughput
The number of work items finished per unit of time — an exact count of items, per day, per week or per Sprint, the period stated.
Throughput versus velocity
Throughput counts finished items; velocity sums the story points of finished items; they answer different questions and are never converted into each other.
Little's Law (1961)
L = λW: in a stable queue the average number of items in the system equals the arrival rate times the average time in the system (John D. C. Little, Operations Research).
Little's Law, flow form
Average WIP = throughput × average cycle time; average cycle time = average WIP ÷ throughput; units must match (items, items per day, days).
Conditions of the flow form (Vacanti, 2015)
Arrival rate equals departure rate · every item that enters eventually leaves · WIP about the same at the start and the end of the period · the average age of WIP neither grows nor shrinks · consistent units.
Average WIP
The mean of the daily counts of items in progress over the period — Team Menu: 31 card-days ÷ 14 days ≈ 2.2 items.
Less WIP, shorter cycle time
At the same throughput, Little's Law gives a shorter average cycle time for a lower average WIP: the limit of Lesson 2 shortens waiting, not work.

Activity 3 · Fun-quiz ×3, computational · 0:42 – 0:47 · 5 min

🎞 Slide 32

Three questions on the screen, one minute each, answer on your phone (Blackboard poll or hands up with fingers). Taking part earns the activity points; the score is for you only. Write the formula before the number.

  1. A board holds 12 items in progress on average and the team finishes 3 items per day. Average cycle time?
  2. A team finishes 5 items per week with an average cycle time of 2 weeks. Average WIP (Work In Progress)?
  3. A ticket is requested (committed) on Monday, started on Wednesday and finished on Friday. Lead time and cycle time, in this course's convention?

In the last minute: the professor works all three on the board, and asks "from when?" at the third one.

LeanVlog · YouTube · ≈ 6 min

The relation of section 3.3 explained with a factory queue, the form in which Little published it; useful to see that the law is not specific to software.

▶
Cycle Time and Little’s Law

The flow form of section 3.3 — average cycle time = WIP ÷ throughput — applied to a team board, with the same units check the fun-quiz asks for (items ÷ items per day = days).

Real-life example 3 · Team Menu's flow table from the Sprint 1 board — lead time, cycle time, age, throughput and one Little's Law line

🎞 Slide 28
The task

Team Menu takes the dates its Sprint 1 board recorded between October 12 and October 25 — committed, started, finished, for each of the four stories — and computes the table that Lab 04 will ask for: lead time and cycle time of every finished story, the age of the unfinished one, the throughput per week, the average WIP (Work In Progress) from the daily counts, and one Little's Law line with the predicted cycle time, the observed one and the reason for the gap. It also writes its counting convention at the top of the table.

Relation to the lecture

It applies section 3.1 (three clocks, elapsed days, the convention), section 3.2 (throughput as a count), section 3.3 (the law and its units) and section 3.4 (the check and its conditions) to the four cards of Lessons 1 and 2 — the same table your team computes in the 35-minute flow block of today's studio, the same line Lab 04 asks for, and the same computation Part C of the Mid-Term asks for with another ticket table.

Convention written at the top of the table: elapsed calendar days; a duration = the later date minus the earlier date; committed = entered Ready at the Sprint Planning of October 12; started = entered In progress; finished = entered Done after the five checks.

Story Points Committed (Ready) Started (In progress) Finished (Done) Lead time Cycle time Age on Oct 25
2 · sesame shown on every dish 1 Mon Oct 12 Tue Oct 13 Fri Oct 16 4 d 3 d —
1 · today's three hot meals 3 Mon Oct 12 Mon Oct 12 Mon Oct 19 7 d 7 d —
3 · an icon next to each allergen 2 Mon Oct 12 Mon Oct 12 Thu Oct 22 10 d 10 d —
4 · the page in French 3 Mon Oct 12 Thu Oct 15 not finished — — 10 d (11 on Oct 26)

Throughput. 3 stories finished in 14 days = 0.21 items per day = 1.5 items per week (1 in the week of October 12, 2 in the week of October 19). Not 6 points per Sprint — that number is the velocity, and it answers a different question.

Average WIP. Cards in progress at the end of each day, October 12 to 25: 2 · 3 · 3 · 4 · 3 · 3 · 3 · 2 · 2 · 2 · 1 · 1 · 1 · 1 — a total of 31 card-days — so the average is 31 ÷ 14 ≈ 2.2 items. The peak, 4, is the Thursday of Activity 1.

The Little's Law line. Predicted average cycle time = 2.2 ÷ 0.21 ≈ 10.3 days. Observed average cycle time of the finished stories = (3 + 7 + 10) ÷ 3 ≈ 6.7 days. They differ because the conditions of the law are not met over this window: it starts with 0 cards and ends with 1 (story 4 entered and did not leave), the sample is four cards, and the average age of the open work grew rather than stayed flat. We will recompute at the end of Sprint 2, over 28 days. That paragraph, in your own words with your own numbers, is the Lab 04 line.

Two readings for the Sprint 2 board. Story 3's cycle time of 10 days contains about five days of waiting — the icons were parked from the 17th while the team worked on the French page. Elapsed time counts them, on purpose: the students waited those days too. And story 4 is the oldest card on the October 26 board, eleven days old against a provisional expectation of ten; the age is the number that tells Noah where to pair on Monday morning, before any new card is pulled.

Where this goes next. The table and the line are the first half of Lab 04 — Flow & Digital Business Brief (opens November 2, feedback November 8); the same shapes appear in Part C of the Mid-Term (November 16) with a ticket table you have not seen, and in the Final.

Team Menu, its members and its data are fictional. Your own board and tables must contain no personal information about anyone outside your team (Legal Notice, section 20).

Code example 3 · Flow metrics calculator — three clocks, throughput and Little's Law

🎞 Slide 33
The task

Takes the four Sprint 1 cards of Team Menu with their three dates, draws each card as a bar on a calendar from October 12 to October 25 — a light segment from committed to started, a solid segment from started to finished, an open-ended segment for the unfinished card — and computes, card by card, lead time, cycle time and age in the course's convention. It then counts the cards in progress at the end of every day, computes the average WIP and the throughput, applies Little's Law, compares the prediction with the observed average, and finishes with the three fun-quiz cases and the class example (WIP 8, throughput 2 per day).

Relation to the lecture

Every step is one definition or one formula of sections 3.1 to 3.4; the picture is Diagram 3 drawn from the data, and the table it fills is the one Lab 04 asks for.

Printed copy: the picture shows the example after its last step. The interactive version (buttons, step-by-step log, downloads) is in the HTML page and in 01_code/ex3_flow_metrics_calculator.html of the companion ZIP.

It then counts the cards in progress at the end of every day, computes the average WIP and the throughput, applies Little's Law, compares the prediction with the observed average cycle time, and finishes with the three fun-quiz cases and the class example (WIP 8, throughput 2 per day). Relation to the lecture: Lesson 3, "Lead time, cycle time, throughput, Little's Law" (sections 3.1 to 3.4; the table Lab 04 asks for and the computation of Part C of the Mid-Term). -->

<script>
// Strict mode: JavaScript reports silent mistakes (for example an undeclared variable) as errors.
"use strict";
// Keeps a copy of this page's source now, before the program changes anything, for the Copy button.
const SOURCE = "<!DOCTYPE html>\n" + document.documentElement.outerHTML;
// The SVG (Scalable Vector Graphics) namespace: every drawing element has to be created in it.
const NS = "http://www.w3.org/2000/svg";
// Shortcut to the drawing surface.
const svg = document.getElementById("viz");
// Shortcut to the execution window.
const logBox = document.getElementById("log");
// Shortcut to the Start/Pause button.
const runBtn = document.getElementById("run");
// Shortcut to the step counter.
const counter = document.getElementById("counter");
// Index of the next step to run (0 means that nothing has run yet).
let next = 0;
// Handle of the repeating timer while the program runs; null while it is paused.
let timer = null;
// The ordered list of steps; each step is a function that does one action and returns the text for the log.
const steps = [];
// Creates one SVG element with the given attributes, attaches it to a parent (default: the drawing) and returns it.
function el(tag, attrs, parent) { const e = document.createElementNS(NS, tag); for (const k in attrs) { e.setAttribute(k, attrs[k]); } (parent || svg).appendChild(e); return e; }
// Writes text at (x, y); the options set size, weight, colour, alignment and parent.
function txt(x, y, s, o) { o = o || {}; const t = el("text", { x: x, y: y, "font-size": o.size || 12, "font-weight": o.weight || 400, fill: o.fill || C.ink, "text-anchor": o.anchor || "start", "font-family": "system-ui, Segoe UI, Roboto, Arial, sans-serif" }, o.parent); t.textContent = s; return t; }
// Splits a sentence into lines of at most max characters, so that it fits inside a box.
function wrap(s, max) { const out = []; let line = ""; for (const w of s.split(" ")) { if ((line + " " + w).trim().length > max) { out.push(line.trim()); line = w; } else { line += " " + w; } } out.push(line.trim()); return out; }
// Brand colours used by the drawing: teal, indigo and rust (a colour-blind-safe set) plus neutral inks.
const C = { teal: "#0A918E", indigo: "#4A3AA7", rust: "#B5440C", ink: "#1B2B2E", muted: "#54646A", line: "#DDD3C4", soft: "#F6F3EE", grid: "#E7E1D6", tealT: "#E4F3F2", indigoT: "#ECEAF7", rustT: "#FBEFE8" };
// Pause between two automatic steps, in milliseconds.
const DELAY = 1800;
// INPUT 1 — the four Sprint 1 cards with their points and three dates in ISO (International Organization for Standardization) format; null = not finished.
const CARDS = [
// Story 2: committed Monday Oct 12, started Tuesday Oct 13, finished Friday Oct 16.
{ id: "2", title: "sesame shown on every dish", pts: 1, committed: "2026-10-12", started: "2026-10-13", finished: "2026-10-16" },
// Story 1: started on the day of the Sprint Planning, finished Monday Oct 19.
{ id: "1", title: "today's three hot meals", pts: 3, committed: "2026-10-12", started: "2026-10-12", finished: "2026-10-19" },
// Story 3: started Oct 12, parked from the 17th, finished Thursday Oct 22.
{ id: "3", title: "an icon next to each allergen", pts: 2, committed: "2026-10-12", started: "2026-10-12", finished: "2026-10-22" },
// Story 4: started Thursday Oct 15, not finished at the end of the Sprint.
{ id: "4", title: "the page in French", pts: 3, committed: "2026-10-12", started: "2026-10-15", finished: null }
// End of the cards.
];
// INPUT 2 — the window of the computation: the first and the last day of Sprint 1 (fourteen days).
const SPRINT = { first: "2026-10-12", last: "2026-10-25" };
// INPUT 3 — the day on which the age of the open card is measured (the last day of the Sprint).
const TODAY = "2026-10-25";
// INPUT 4 — the three fun-quiz cases of Activity 3 (each case names what is known and what is asked).
const QUIZ = [
// Case 1: WIP and throughput known, cycle time asked.
{ q: "12 items in progress on average, 3 finished per day → average cycle time?", wip: 12, tp: 3, unit: "day" },
// Case 2: throughput and cycle time known, WIP asked.
{ q: "5 items finished per week, average cycle time 2 weeks → average WIP?", tp: 5, ct: 2, unit: "week" },
// Case 3: three dates known, lead time and cycle time asked (Monday → Wednesday → Friday).
{ q: "committed Monday, started Wednesday, finished Friday → lead time and cycle time?", committed: "2026-10-19", started: "2026-10-21", finished: "2026-10-23" }
// End of the quiz cases.
];
// INPUT 5 — the class example of section 3.3: eight items in progress, two finished per day.
const CLASS_EXAMPLE = { wip: 8, tp: 2 };
// Number of milliseconds in one day, used to turn a difference of dates into days.
const MS_DAY = 86400000;
// Turns an ISO date into a Date object at midnight UTC (Coordinated Universal Time), so that daylight-saving changes cannot shift a day.
function iso(s) { return new Date(s + "T00:00:00Z"); }
// THE COUNTING CONVENTION OF THE COURSE, in one function: the later date minus the earlier date, in whole days (Mon → Fri = 4). Add 1 here for inclusive counting.
function days(a, b) { return Math.round((iso(b) - iso(a)) / MS_DAY); }
// Short label of an ISO date, for example "Oct 16".
function label(s) { const d = iso(s); return ["Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "May", "Jun", "Jul", "Aug", "Sep", "Oct", "Nov", "Dec"][d.getUTCMonth()] + " " + d.getUTCDate(); }
// Weekday letter of an ISO date (S M T W T F S).
function wd(s) { return "SMTWTFS"[iso(s).getUTCDay()]; }
// The ISO date n days after the first day of the Sprint.
function dayN(n) { const d = new Date(iso(SPRINT.first).getTime() + n * MS_DAY); return d.toISOString().slice(0, 10); }
// Number of days drawn on the calendar (14).
const NDAYS = days(SPRINT.first, SPRINT.last) + 1;
// Geometry of the calendar: left edge, width of one day, top of the first row, height of one row.
const G = { x0: 206, dw: 38, y0: 58, rh: 38 };
// x position of the start of a given ISO date on the calendar.
function dx(s) { return G.x0 + days(SPRINT.first, s) * G.dw; }
// Little's Law in its flow form: average cycle time = average WIP ÷ throughput (same time unit as the throughput).
function littlesLaw(wip, tp) { return wip / tp; }
// Draws the calendar: title, fourteen day columns with weekday letters and dates, one row per card, and the frame of the WIP chart.
function drawCalendar() {
// Removes everything drawn before (needed by Restart).
svg.innerHTML = "";
// Title.
txt(16, 20, "Team Menu · Sprint 1 cards on the calendar · convention: a duration = later date − earlier date (elapsed calendar days)", { size: 11.5, weight: 700 });
// Day columns: alternating light background for the weekend, letter and date on top.
for (let n = 0; n < NDAYS; n++) { const s = dayN(n); const x = G.x0 + n * G.dw; const we = wd(s) === "S"; el("rect", { x: x, y: 30, width: G.dw, height: 190, fill: we ? "#F1ECE4" : (n % 2 ? "#FBF9F6" : "#fff"), stroke: C.grid }); txt(x + G.dw / 2, 41, wd(s), { size: 8.5, fill: C.muted, anchor: "middle" }); txt(x + G.dw / 2, 52, String(iso(s).getUTCDate()), { size: 9.5, weight: 700, anchor: "middle" }); }
// Month label on the left of the header.
txt(16, 46, "October 2026", { size: 10, weight: 700, fill: C.muted });
// One row per card: label area on the left (title, points), empty for the moment.
CARDS.forEach(function (c, i) { const y = G.y0 + i * G.rh; txt(16, y + 14, "#" + c.id + " · " + c.pts + " pt · " + c.title, { size: 9, weight: 700 }); el("line", { x1: 16, y1: y + G.rh - 2, x2: 744, y2: y + G.rh - 2, stroke: C.grid }); });
// Legend under the rows.
txt(16, 236, "dot = committed · light dashed = committed → started (waiting in Ready) · solid = started → finished (cycle time) · rust arrow = still in progress (age)", { size: 8.2, fill: C.muted });
// The WIP chart frame: caption and baseline.
txt(16, 262, "Cards in progress at the end of each day (WIP)", { size: 10, weight: 700 });
// Baseline of the WIP columns.
el("line", { x1: G.x0, y1: 318, x2: G.x0 + NDAYS * G.dw, y2: 318, stroke: C.muted });
// Numbers area: a frame for the results on the lower part of the drawing.
el("rect", { x: 16, y: 334, width: 728, height: 178, rx: 10, fill: C.soft, stroke: C.line });
// Heading of the numbers area.
txt(26, 352, "Results", { size: 10.5, weight: 800, fill: C.muted });
// End of drawCalendar.
}
// Draws one card's bar: light segment committed → started, solid segment started → finished, or an open rust segment to today.
function drawCard(c, i) { const y = G.y0 + i * G.rh + 18; const xc = dx(c.committed), xs = dx(c.started); if (xs > xc) { el("rect", { x: xc, y: y, width: xs - xc, height: 12, fill: C.tealT, stroke: C.teal, "stroke-dasharray": "3 2" }); } if (c.finished) { el("rect", { x: xs, y: y, width: dx(c.finished) - xs, height: 12, fill: C.teal }); el("circle", { cx: dx(c.finished), cy: y + 6, r: 4, fill: "#fff", stroke: C.teal, "stroke-width": 2 }); } else { const xe = dx(TODAY) + G.dw; el("rect", { x: xs, y: y, width: xe - xs - 10, height: 12, fill: C.rust }); el("path", { d: "M" + (xe - 10) + " " + (y - 2) + " L" + xe + " " + (y + 6) + " L" + (xe - 10) + " " + (y + 14) + " Z", fill: C.rust }); } el("circle", { cx: xc, cy: y + 6, r: 3, fill: C.indigo }); }
// Writes a card's three numbers under its label, in the label area.
function writeNumbers(i, s) { const y = G.y0 + i * G.rh; txt(16, y + 27, s, { size: 8.5, fill: C.muted }); }
// Counts the cards in progress at the end of a day: started on or before the day, and finished after it (or not finished).
function wipOn(s) { return CARDS.filter(function (c) { return days(c.started, s) >= 0 && (c.finished === null || days(s, c.finished) > 0); }).length; }
// Draws one WIP column for one day.
function drawWipColumn(n, w) { const x = G.x0 + n * G.dw; el("rect", { x: x + 6, y: 318 - w * 11, width: G.dw - 12, height: w * 11, fill: w === 4 ? C.rust : C.indigo }); txt(x + G.dw / 2, 318 - w * 11 - 3, String(w), { size: 9, weight: 700, anchor: "middle" }); }
// Writes one result line in the numbers area (row 0 to 7).
function result(row, s, o) { o = o || {}; return txt(26 + (o.col || 0) * 392, 370 + row * 17, s, { size: o.size || 9.5, weight: o.weight || 400, fill: o.fill || C.ink }); }
// Builds the ordered list of steps.
function buildSteps() {
// Empties the list (needed by Restart).
steps.length = 0;
// Step 1: what the program will do.
steps.push(function () { return "Start · four cards, three dates each; the program draws them on the calendar, computes the three clocks in the course's convention, counts the daily WIP, computes throughput and average WIP, applies Little's Law and compares it with what the board observed."; });
// Step 2: inputs and the convention.
steps.push(function () { return "Inputs · window " + label(SPRINT.first) + " → " + label(SPRINT.last) + " (" + NDAYS + " days) · age measured on " + label(TODAY) + " · convention in days(a, b) = later date − earlier date: days('2026-10-12', '2026-10-16') = " + days("2026-10-12", "2026-10-16") + " (Mon → Fri = 4). For inclusive counting, add 1 in that one function and every number below shifts by one."; });
// Step 3: the calendar.
steps.push(function () { drawCalendar(); return "Calendar drawn · one column per day (weekends shaded), one row per card; the label area on the left will receive each card's numbers."; });
// Steps 4 to 7: one per card.
CARDS.forEach(function (c, i) { steps.push(function () { drawCard(c, i); if (c.finished) { const lead = days(c.committed, c.finished), cycle = days(c.started, c.finished); writeNumbers(i, "lead " + lead + " d · cycle " + cycle + " d" + (lead > cycle ? " · waited " + (lead - cycle) + " d in Ready" : " · no waiting")); return "Card #" + c.id + " · lead time = finished − committed = " + label(c.finished) + " − " + label(c.committed) + " = " + lead + " days · cycle time = finished − started = " + label(c.finished) + " − " + label(c.started) + " = " + cycle + " days" + (lead > cycle ? " · the difference (" + (lead - cycle) + " d) is the time the card waited in Ready." : " · no waiting: started on the day it was committed."); } const age = days(c.started, TODAY); writeNumbers(i, "open · age " + age + " d on " + label(TODAY) + " · " + (age + 1) + " d on Oct 26"); return "Card #" + c.id + " · not finished: lead time and cycle time do not exist yet (both clocks are still running). Work item age = today − started = " + label(TODAY) + " − " + label(c.started) + " = " + age + " days (" + (age + 1) + " on Monday October 26). It is the oldest card on the board: that is where the pairing goes first."; }); });
// Step 8: the daily WIP counts.
steps.push(function () { const counts = []; for (let n = 0; n < NDAYS; n++) { const w = wipOn(dayN(n)); counts.push(w); drawWipColumn(n, w); } const sum = counts.reduce(function (a, b) { return a + b; }, 0); return "Daily WIP · cards started on or before the day and not yet finished: " + counts.join(" · ") + " → " + sum + " card-days in " + NDAYS + " days. The peak (4) is Thursday October 15, the day of Activity 1. The window opened with 0 cards in progress on the morning of Oct 12 (end of that day: " + counts[0] + ") and closes with " + counts[counts.length - 1] + " on the evening of Oct 25."; });
// Step 9: average WIP.
steps.push(function () { let sum = 0; for (let n = 0; n < NDAYS; n++) { sum += wipOn(dayN(n)); } const avg = sum / NDAYS; result(0, "Average WIP = " + sum + " card-days ÷ " + NDAYS + " days = " + avg.toFixed(2) + " items", { weight: 700 }); return "Average WIP = " + sum + " ÷ " + NDAYS + " = " + avg.toFixed(2) + " items (read it off the chart: the mean height of the fourteen columns)."; });
// Step 10: throughput.
steps.push(function () { const done = CARDS.filter(function (c) { return c.finished; }).length; const tp = done / NDAYS; result(1, "Throughput = " + done + " finished ÷ " + NDAYS + " days = " + tp.toFixed(3) + " items/day = " + (tp * 7).toFixed(2) + " items/week", { weight: 700 }); return "Throughput = " + done + " items finished ÷ " + NDAYS + " days = " + tp.toFixed(3) + " items per day = " + (tp * 7).toFixed(1) + " items per week (1 in the week of Oct 12, 2 in the week of Oct 19). It counts items, not points: 6 points per Sprint is the velocity, a different question."; });
// Step 11: Little's Law prediction.
steps.push(function () { let sum = 0; for (let n = 0; n < NDAYS; n++) { sum += wipOn(dayN(n)); } const avg = sum / NDAYS; const done = CARDS.filter(function (c) { return c.finished; }).length; const tp = done / NDAYS; const pred = littlesLaw(avg, tp); result(2, "Little's Law: predicted average cycle time = " + avg.toFixed(2) + " ÷ " + tp.toFixed(3) + " = " + pred.toFixed(1) + " days", { weight: 700, fill: C.indigo }); return "Little's Law (flow form): average cycle time = average WIP ÷ throughput = " + avg.toFixed(2) + " items ÷ " + tp.toFixed(3) + " items/day = " + pred.toFixed(1) + " days. Units check: items ÷ (items/day) = days."; });
// Step 12: observed average and the gap.
steps.push(function () { const fin = CARDS.filter(function (c) { return c.finished; }); const cts = fin.map(function (c) { return days(c.started, c.finished); }); const obs = cts.reduce(function (a, b) { return a + b; }, 0) / cts.length; result(3, "Observed average cycle time of the finished cards = (" + cts.join(" + ") + ") ÷ " + cts.length + " = " + obs.toFixed(1) + " days", { weight: 700, fill: C.rust }); wrap("Gap: the conditions of the law are not met over this window — it opens with 0 cards in progress and closes with 1 (story 4 entered and did not leave), the sample is four cards, and the age of the open work grew instead of staying flat. Recompute at the end of Sprint 2, over 28 days.", 80).forEach(function (l, k) { result(4 + k, l, { size: 8.5, fill: C.muted }); }); return "Observed average cycle time = (" + cts.join(" + ") + ") ÷ " + cts.length + " = " + obs.toFixed(1) + " days, against a prediction of about 10 days. The gap is not an error of arithmetic: Little's Law holds for averages of a system in which what enters also leaves. Here (1) the window opens with 0 cards in progress and closes with 1, so what entered did not all leave, (2) story 4 entered and never left, (3) four cards are a tiny sample. The Lab 04 line states the two numbers and this reason."; });
// Steps 13 to 15: the fun-quiz cases.
steps.push(function () { const q = QUIZ[0]; const ct = littlesLaw(q.wip, q.tp); result(1, "Quiz 1: " + q.wip + " ÷ " + q.tp + " = " + ct + " days", { col: 1, weight: 700 }); return "Fun-quiz 1 · " + q.q + " → cycle time = WIP ÷ throughput = " + q.wip + " ÷ " + q.tp + " = " + ct + " days (items ÷ items per day = days)."; });
// Case 2 (the unknown is the WIP).
steps.push(function () { const q = QUIZ[1]; const wip = q.tp * q.ct; result(2, "Quiz 2: " + q.tp + " × " + q.ct + " = " + wip + " items", { col: 1, weight: 700 }); return "Fun-quiz 2 · " + q.q + " → WIP = throughput × cycle time = " + q.tp + " × " + q.ct + " = " + wip + " items (items per week × weeks = items). Dividing gives 2.5 — the common error: ask which quantity is unknown."; });
// Case 3 (three dates).
steps.push(function () { const q = QUIZ[2]; const lead = days(q.committed, q.finished), cycle = days(q.started, q.finished); result(3, "Quiz 3: lead " + lead + " d · cycle " + cycle + " d", { col: 1, weight: 700 }); return "Fun-quiz 3 · " + q.q + " → lead time = Friday − Monday = " + lead + " days; cycle time = Friday − Wednesday = " + cycle + " days (difference of dates). Inclusive counting would give 5 and 3 — acceptable if said aloud. 'From when?' is the question that decides."; });
// Step 16: the class example and the end.
steps.push(function () { const ct = littlesLaw(CLASS_EXAMPLE.wip, CLASS_EXAMPLE.tp); result(0, "Class example: " + CLASS_EXAMPLE.wip + " items ÷ " + CLASS_EXAMPLE.tp + " items/day = " + ct + " days", { col: 1, weight: 700, fill: C.indigo }); return "Class example · " + CLASS_EXAMPLE.wip + " items in progress on average, " + CLASS_EXAMPLE.tp + " finished per day → average cycle time " + ct + " days. Done · the clean cases agree with the law because their inputs are averages of a stable system; Team Menu's window is not one yet. Try: give story 4 the finished date 2026-10-25 and press Restart."; });
// End of buildSteps.
}
// Restart: stops, clears the log, draws the empty calendar, rebuilds the steps and returns to step 0.
function restart() { pause(); next = 0; logBox.innerHTML = ""; drawCalendar(); buildSteps(); counter.textContent = "Step 0 / " + steps.length; runBtn.textContent = "▶ Start"; }
// Writes one numbered line in the execution window, highlights it and scrolls down to it.
function log(text) { const prev = logBox.querySelector(".now"); if (prev) { prev.classList.remove("now"); } const d = document.createElement("div"); d.className = "now"; d.textContent = String(next).padStart(2, "0") + " │ " + text; logBox.appendChild(d); logBox.scrollTop = logBox.scrollHeight; }
// Runs the next step, writes its result, updates the counter, and stops by itself after the last step.
function stepOnce() { if (next >= steps.length) { pause(); return; } const text = steps[next](); next += 1; log(text); counter.textContent = "Step " + next + " / " + steps.length; if (next >= steps.length) { pause(); runBtn.textContent = "✓ Finished"; } }
// Starts (or resumes) the automatic run: one step now, then one step every DELAY milliseconds.
function start() { if (next >= steps.length) { return; } runBtn.textContent = "⏸ Pause"; stepOnce(); if (next < steps.length) { timer = setInterval(stepOnce, DELAY); } }
// Pauses the automatic run; the next Start continues from exactly the same step.
function pause() { clearInterval(timer); timer = null; if (next < steps.length) { runBtn.textContent = "▶ Start"; } }
// Copies SOURCE to the clipboard; if the browser blocks the Clipboard API (Application Programming Interface), a hidden text area is used instead.
function copyCode() { const b = document.getElementById("copy"); const done = function () { b.textContent = "✓ Copied"; setTimeout(function () { b.textContent = "⧉ Copy code"; }, 1500); }; const fallback = function () { const t = document.createElement("textarea"); t.value = SOURCE; document.body.appendChild(t); t.select(); document.execCommand("copy"); t.remove(); done(); }; if (navigator.clipboard && window.isSecureContext) { navigator.clipboard.writeText(SOURCE).then(done, fallback); } else { fallback(); } }
// Serializes the drawing as it is now into a self-contained SVG text (with the XML namespace and a white background).
function svgText() { const clone = svg.cloneNode(true); clone.setAttribute("xmlns", NS); const bg = document.createElementNS(NS, "rect"); bg.setAttribute("width", "100%"); bg.setAttribute("height", "100%"); bg.setAttribute("fill", "#FFFFFF"); clone.insertBefore(bg, clone.firstChild); return '<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>\n' + new XMLSerializer().serializeToString(clone); }
// Triggers a browser download of the given text or blob under the given file name.
function download(name, data, type) { const blob = data instanceof Blob ? data : new Blob([data], { type: type }); const url = URL.createObjectURL(blob); const a = document.createElement("a"); a.href = url; a.download = name; document.body.appendChild(a); a.click(); a.remove(); setTimeout(function () { URL.revokeObjectURL(url); }, 1000); }
// Download SVG button: saves the current drawing as a vector file.
document.getElementById("dlsvg").addEventListener("click", function () { download("ex3_flow_metrics_calculator.svg", svgText(), "image/svg+xml"); });
// Download PNG button: draws the current SVG on a hidden canvas at double resolution, then saves it as a picture file.
document.getElementById("dlpng").addEventListener("click", function () { const img = new Image(); const url = URL.createObjectURL(new Blob([svgText()], { type: "image/svg+xml" })); img.onload = function () { const c = document.createElement("canvas"); c.width = 760 * 2; c.height = 520 * 2; const g = c.getContext("2d"); g.fillStyle = "#FFFFFF"; g.fillRect(0, 0, c.width, c.height); g.drawImage(img, 0, 0, c.width, c.height); URL.revokeObjectURL(url); c.toBlob(function (b) { download("ex3_flow_metrics_calculator.png", b, "image/png"); }, "image/png"); }; img.src = url; });
// Start/Pause button: pauses if the program is running, otherwise starts or resumes it.
runBtn.addEventListener("click", function () { if (timer) { pause(); } else { start(); } });
// Next-step button: works only while paused, so the class sets the pace.
document.getElementById("stepBtn").addEventListener("click", function () { if (!timer) { stepOnce(); } });
// Restart button.
document.getElementById("reset").addEventListener("click", restart);
// Copy-code button.
document.getElementById("copy").addEventListener("click", copyCode);
// Draws the starting state as soon as the page is loaded.
restart();
// End of the program.
</script>
<!-- End of the visible page. -->
</body>
<!-- End of the document. -->
</html>

Step by step — what the program does

  1. Inputs. CARDS holds the four stories with their points and three dates (ISO format); SPRINT holds the first and last day; QUIZ holds the three fun-quiz cases and CLASS_EXAMPLE the WIP 8 ÷ 2 case; days(a, b) returns the difference of two dates in whole days — the counting convention of the course, in one function you can change.
  2. The calendar. drawCalendar() draws one column per day from October 12 to 25 and one row per card; drawCard() draws the committed→started segment in light teal, the started→finished segment in solid teal, and an open-ended rust segment with an arrow for the card that is still in progress.
  3. One step per card. Each step computes lead = days(committed, finished), cycle = days(started, finished) and, for an unfinished card, age = days(started, today), writes the three numbers at the end of the bar and prints the subtraction in the log — for example 'Oct 16 − Oct 13 = 3 days'.
  4. Daily WIP. One step walks the fourteen days, counts the cards whose started date is on or before the day and whose finished date is after it (or empty), draws the count as a small column under the calendar and sums the card-days; the next step divides the sum by 14.
  5. Throughput and the law. The finished cards are counted and divided by 14 days (and expressed per week); littlesLaw() divides the average WIP by the throughput, the observed average cycle time is computed from the finished cards, and the log prints both numbers with the three reasons for the gap.
  6. Clean cases. The last steps run the three fun-quiz cases and the class example through the same two functions, so the class sees the law agree when the inputs are averages of a stable system.
  7. Controls. Start / Pause / Next step / Restart / Copy / ⤓ SVG / ⤓ PNG, as in Example 1. Pause after the daily-WIP step and ask the class to read the average off the picture before the next step prints it.
  8. Try it. In the copied code, give story 4 a finished date of 2026-10-25 and press Restart: the window now ends with 0 cards in progress, the observed average changes, and the gap to the prediction shrinks — then change days() to add 1 (inclusive counting) and watch every number shift by one.

Buttons: ▶ Start / ⏸ Pause (resumes where it stopped), ⏭ Next step, ↺ Restart, ⧉ Copy code, ⤓ SVG / ⤓ PNG (download the picture as it is now); every step is written in the execution window. A comment line precedes every line of code. Educational example, provided as is for your own study (Legal Notice, sections 4.2 and 11).

Flash-cards · Lesson 3 · click a card to flip it

Card 3.1 · question

Cycle time and work item age (Kanban Guide)?

Answer

Cycle time: the elapsed time between when a work item started and when it finished. Work item age: the elapsed time between when it started and the current date — the same clock, read before the item has finished.

Card 3.2 · question

Lead time, in this course?

Answer

The elapsed time from the commitment point (the card entered Ready) to the delivery point (Done) — the clock the person who was promised the item experiences.

Card 3.3 · question

A card started on Monday and finished on Friday — cycle time in this course's convention?

Answer

4 days: the finish date minus the start date (some teams count inclusively and say 5; the convention is written in the Definition of Workflow).

Card 3.4 · question

Throughput, and how it differs from velocity?

Answer

Throughput: the number of work items finished per unit of time — an exact count of items. Velocity: the sum of the story points of the finished stories. Items versus points; never converted.

Card 3.5 · question

Little's Law in its flow form, with the class example?

Answer

Average cycle time = average WIP ÷ throughput. WIP 8 items, throughput 2 items per day → 4 days. Units must match.

Card 3.6 · question

The five conditions of Little's Law's flow form (Vacanti)?

Answer

Arrival rate = departure rate · every item that enters leaves · WIP about the same at the start and the end · the average age of WIP neither grows nor shrinks · consistent units.

Lesson 4 · The cumulative flow diagram, and Scrum vs. Kanban vs. Scrumban

0:47 – 0:57 · 10 minutes, then activity 0:57 – 1:00🎞 Slide 34

By the end of this lesson you can

  • Read a cumulative flow diagram: the thickness of a band is the WIP of that state, the horizontal distance between the top and bottom lines is the approximate lead time, the slope of the bottom line is the throughput, and a band that widens is the state where work accumulates.
  • Write a Service Level Expectation with its two parts — a period and a probability — from historical cycle times, and say why a three-card sample makes it provisional.
  • Compare Scrum, Kanban and Scrumban on roles, events, artifacts, time-boxes, how work enters, how WIP is controlled and what is measured, and choose one for a given kind of work in five sentences with reasons.

4.1 · The cumulative flow diagram

🎞 Slides 35–36

Everything measured in Lesson 3 can be shown in one picture. A CFD (Cumulative Flow Diagram) counts, for every day, how many work items have entered each state since the beginning — committed, started, finished — and draws those cumulative counts as stacked bands: the finished items at the bottom, then the items in progress, then the items committed but not started. Because the counts are cumulative, every line can only go up or stay flat; the reading is in the distances between the lines.

Three distances carry the three numbers. The vertical thickness of a band on a given day is the number of items in that state on that day — the band in the middle is the WIP (Work In Progress) of Lesson 2, read directly. The horizontal distance between the top line (committed) and the bottom line (finished), at a given height, is the approximate time an item committed on that day took to be finished — the approximate average lead time of Lesson 3. The slope of the bottom line is the throughput: how many items were finished per day. From those three readings come the diagnoses. Bands of constant thickness, lines roughly parallel: a stable flow. A band that widens — its top line rising faster than its bottom line — is a state where items arrive faster than they leave: a bottleneck, and the place to look. A bottom line that goes flat for days: nothing is being finished, whatever else is moving. The Companion's own drill is one example: an In progress band that widens from four to ten while the finished line stays flat is a team that starts faster than it finishes; the answer is to lower the limit, swarm on finishing, and look for the blocked items.

The diagram needs no tool. Team Menu's Sprint 1 produces one with three lines from the table of Lesson 3: four items committed on October 12 (the top line jumps to 4 and stays there), the started line reaching 4 on October 15, the finished line stepping to 1, 2 and 3 on October 16, 19 and 22. With four cards it is a small picture, but it already shows the band in the middle at its widest on October 15 — the day of Activity 1 — and the finished line flat for the last three days.

4.2 · The Service Level Expectation

🎞 Slide 37

The sixth element of the DoW (Definition of Workflow) is the SLE (Service Level Expectation): in the Kanban Guide's words, "a forecast of how long it should take a work item to flow from started to finished", which "has two parts: a period of elapsed time and a probability associated with that period", and which "should be based on historical cycle time" (kanbanguides.org). "85 % of our stories are finished within 8 days of being started" is an SLE (Service Level Expectation); "we try to be quick" is not. It is a forecast, not a promise, and it is computed from the team's own cycle times — which is why Team Menu's first one, written from three cycle times of 3, 7 and 10 days, is provisional — "within 10 days, about 85 % of the time", in pencil — until Sprint 2 has added its cards. An SLE (Service Level Expectation) is what turns a card's age into a decision: a card older than the expectation is the card to help today.

4.3 · Scrum, Kanban, Scrumban — which, for which work?

🎞 Slides 38–39

You now hold two complete vocabularies, and the comparison is factual, not a matter of taste. Scrum (the Scrum Guide 2020) is a framework: it prescribes three accountabilities, five events inside a Sprint of one month or less, three artifacts with their commitments, and a Sprint Goal that does not change during the Sprint; work enters at Sprint Planning. Kanban (the Kanban Guide; the Kanban Method) is a strategy for optimizing flow: it prescribes no roles, no events and no artifacts; work enters continuously, pulled when there is capacity; WIP (Work In Progress) is controlled by explicit limits; policies may change at any moment by decision; what is measured is WIP (Work In Progress), throughput, work item age, cycle time and the SLE (Service Level Expectation). Scrumban is the name Corey Ladas gave in 2008, and in his 2009 book, to a Scrum team that adopts Kanban's pull, limits and flow measures while keeping Scrum (Modus Cooperandi); Scrum.org's own Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams describes the same combination from the other side — the Scrum events and accountabilities unchanged, a Definition of Workflow and the four flow metrics added (scrum.org). Scrumban is not half of Scrum; it is all of Scrum plus the practices of this hour.

Which one, then? The question is the kind of work, not the quality of the team. When work can be planned into a goal for a time-box and the stakeholders gain from a regular rhythm of review and replanning — a product built in increments, like yours — Scrum fits. When work arrives continuously and unpredictably, in independent items that cannot wait for a planning day — support requests, operations, maintenance — Kanban fits, and Anderson's first system was built for exactly that stream. When a Scrum team finds that its Sprints hide queues, that too much is started at once, and that it wants cycle times and ages next to its velocity without losing its rhythm, Scrumban fits — which is Team Menu's situation after Sprint 1, and probably yours.

The studio asks each team for a decision memo: five sentences, each with a reason. Team Menu's reads: (1) We keep Scrum, because our work can be planned into a Sprint Goal and the cafeteria manager wants to inspect an increment every two weeks. (2) We add WIP limits — In progress ≤ 2, Review ≤ 1 — because Sprint 1 ended with four stories started and three finished. (3) Inside the Sprint we pull from a Ready column refilled by the Product Owner at the Daily Scrum, instead of everyone starting a story on day one. (4) At each Sprint Review we read throughput, cycle time and the age of the open cards next to the velocity. (5) Therefore Scrumban from October 26, to be reviewed at the Retrospective of November 8. Five sentences, five reasons, one date.

4.4 · Reading the hand-out and the flash-cards

Diagram 4 in your hand-out has the generic eight-week CFD (Cumulative Flow Diagram) with its widening band, Team Menu's small one, and the three-column comparison; the reference table in the ZIP has every row. Activity 4 closes the hour with the six words of the week on flash-cards, and sixty seconds of silence before the quiz: attention is a resource, and we have just spent an hour on why a resource should not be split four ways.

Terms to learn

Cumulative Flow Diagram (CFD)
A chart of the cumulative number of items that have entered each state, day by day, drawn as stacked bands — finished at the bottom, in progress above, committed on top.
Band thickness
The vertical distance across a band on a given day = the number of items in that state that day; the middle band is the WIP.
Horizontal distance
The distance between the top line (committed) and the bottom line (finished) at a given height = the approximate average lead time of the items committed that day.
Slope of the finished line
Items finished per day = the throughput; a flat stretch means nothing was finished.
Widening band / bottleneck
A band whose top line rises faster than its bottom line: items enter that state faster than they leave it — the place to look first.
Service Level Expectation (SLE)
A forecast of how long a work item should take from started to finished, with two parts — a period and a probability — based on historical cycle time (Kanban Guide): '85 % within 8 days'.
Provisional SLE
An SLE written from very few cycle times (Team Menu: three), kept in pencil and recomputed as data accumulates; a forecast, never a promise.
Scrum (framework)
Three accountabilities, five events in a Sprint of one month or less, three artifacts with commitments, a Sprint Goal fixed for the Sprint; work enters at Sprint Planning (Scrum Guide 2020).
Kanban (strategy / method)
No prescribed roles, events or artifacts; continuous pull when there is capacity; explicit WIP limits and policies; measures: WIP, throughput, work item age, cycle time, SLE.
Scrumban
Corey Ladas's name (2008–2009) for a Scrum team that adopts Kanban's pull, WIP limits and flow measures while keeping Scrum — all of Scrum plus the practices of this hour.
Kind of work
The criterion for choosing: plannable into a time-boxed goal with stakeholders who want a rhythm → Scrum; continuous, unpredictable, independent items → Kanban; a Scrum team that wants flow without losing its rhythm → Scrumban.
Decision memo
Five sentences, each with a reason, ending with a method and a date for reviewing the decision (the studio's last block today).

Real-life example 4 · Team Menu draws its Sprint 1 cumulative flow diagram, writes a provisional SLE, and decides: Scrumban

🎞 Slide 36
The task

Team Menu builds the three cumulative lines of its Sprint 1 — committed, started, finished — day by day from the table of Lesson 3, reads the three distances off the picture, compares the small diagram with a generic eight-week one that shows a widening band, writes its first SLE (Service Level Expectation) in pencil from its three cycle times, and completes the five-sentence decision memo that closes today's studio.

Relation to the lecture

It applies section 4.1 (how a CFD is built and read), section 4.2 (the two parts of an SLE and why a small sample keeps it provisional) and section 4.3 (the comparison and the memo) to the data of Lessons 1 to 3 — the same sketch and the same memo your team produces in the studio and keeps in the team folder for the Mid-Term's Part D.

Cumulative counts, Sprint 1 (items that have entered the state, end of day).

Date Committed (Ready or beyond) Started (In progress or beyond) Finished (Done) Band: in Ready Band: in progress (WIP)
Mon Oct 12 4 2 0 2 2
Tue Oct 13 4 3 0 1 3
Wed Oct 14 4 3 0 1 3
Thu Oct 15 4 4 0 0 4
Fri Oct 16 4 4 1 0 3
Sat Oct 17 – Sun Oct 18 4 4 1 0 3
Mon Oct 19 4 4 2 0 2
Tue Oct 20 – Wed Oct 21 4 4 2 0 2
Thu Oct 22 4 4 3 0 1
Fri Oct 23 – Sun Oct 25 4 4 3 0 1

The three readings. Thickness: the middle band is widest on October 15 — four items, the whole Sprint content, in progress at once. Horizontal distance: from the committed line (4 since October 12) to the finished line, the gaps are 4, 7 and 10 days for the first, second and third item — the lead times of Lesson 3, read on the picture. Slope: the finished line rises by one item on October 16, 19 and 22 — about one every three days, 0.21 per day — and is flat from October 22 to 25: nothing finished in the last three days while story 4 stayed open. The generic eight-week diagram of Example 4 shows what the same reading looks like with more cards: an In progress band widening from one to twelve while the finished line slows to one item per week — the Companion's drill — and the diagnosis is the same as Lesson 2's: lower the limit, swarm, find what is blocked.

The provisional SLE. Cycle times so far: 3, 7 and 10 days. With three values no percentile means much, so the team writes, in pencil: "a story should be finished within 10 days of being started, about 85 % of the time — provisional; recompute on November 8 from the Sprint 1 + Sprint 2 cards." The expectation already has a use on October 26: story 4 is eleven days old, above the line, and that is where the pairing goes first.

The decision memo (five sentences). (1) We keep Scrum, because our work can be planned into a Sprint Goal and the cafeteria manager wants to inspect an increment every two weeks. (2) We add WIP (Work In Progress) limits — In progress ≤ 2, Review ≤ 1 — because Sprint 1 ended with four stories started and three finished. (3) Inside the Sprint we pull from a Ready column that the Product Owner refills at the Daily Scrum, instead of everyone starting a story on day one. (4) At each Sprint Review we read throughput, cycle time and the age of the open cards next to the velocity. (5) Therefore Scrumban from October 26, to be reviewed at the Retrospective of November 8.

Where this goes next. The sketch and the memo stay in the team folder; Part D of the Mid-Term (November 16) gives you a scenario and asks Scrum or Kanban, with reasons — the same five-sentence shape; the Final asks you to read a CFD (Cumulative Flow Diagram) with a bottleneck.

Team Menu, its members and its data are fictional. Your own board and tables must contain no personal information about anyone outside your team (Legal Notice, section 20).

Code example 4 · Cumulative flow diagram builder and method chooser

🎞 Slide 41
The task

Builds Team Menu's Sprint 1 cumulative flow diagram one day at a time from the three dates of each card — the committed, started and finished lines and the two bands between them — and reads the three distances aloud in the log (thickness = WIP, horizontal gap = lead time, bottom slope = throughput). It then draws a generic eight-week diagram with four states in which the In progress band widens while the finished line slows, names the bottleneck, and finally scores a short decision checklist for Team Menu's kind of work to arrive at Scrumban.

Relation to the lecture

The first part is section 4.1 drawn from the Lesson 3 data; the eight-week diagram is the Companion's drill; the checklist is section 4.3 made explicit — the three questions about the kind of work and the five-sentence memo.

Printed copy: the picture shows the example after its last step. The interactive version (buttons, step-by-step log, downloads) is in the HTML page and in 01_code/ex4_cfd_and_method_chooser.html of the companion ZIP.

It then draws a generic eight-week diagram with four states in which the In progress band widens while the finished line slows, names the bottleneck, and finally scores a three-question decision checklist for Team Menu's kind of work to arrive at Scrumban with its five-sentence memo. { q: "Can the work be planned into a goal for a time-box, and do the stakeholders gain from a regular rhythm of review?", a: "Yes — the cafeteria manager inspects an increment every two weeks; the stories can be planned into a Sprint Goal.", votes: "scrum" },

];

"(1) We keep Scrum: our work can be planned into a Sprint Goal and the cafeteria manager wants to inspect an increment every two weeks.",
// Sentence 2.
"(2) We add WIP limits — In progress ≤ 2, Review ≤ 1 — because Sprint 1 ended with four stories started and three finished.",
// Sentence 3.
"(3) Inside the Sprint we pull from a Ready column that the Product Owner refills at the Daily Scrum, instead of everyone starting a story on day one.",

];

// Number of milliseconds in one day.
const MS_DAY = 86400000;
// Turns an ISO date into a Date at midnight UTC (Coordinated Universal Time).
function iso(s) { return new Date(s + "T00:00:00Z"); }
// The counting convention of the course: later date minus earlier date, in whole days.
function days(a, b) { return Math.round((iso(b) - iso(a)) / MS_DAY); }
// The ISO date n days after the first day of the Sprint.
function dayN(n) { return new Date(iso(SPRINT.first).getTime() + n * MS_DAY).toISOString().slice(0, 10); }
// Short label of an ISO date, for example "Oct 16".
function label(s) { const d = iso(s); return "Oct " + d.getUTCDate(); }
// Number of days in Team Menu's diagram (14).
const NDAYS = days(SPRINT.first, SPRINT.last) + 1;
// CUMULATIVE COUNTS for one day: how many cards have entered each state on or before that day (the core of a cumulative flow diagram).
function cumulative(s) { return { committed: CARDS.filter(function (c) { return days(c.committed, s) >= 0; }).length, started: CARDS.filter(function (c) { return days(c.started, s) >= 0; }).length, finished: CARDS.filter(function (c) { return c.finished !== null && days(c.finished, s) >= 0; }).length }; }

const B = { x: 430, y: 48, w: 300, h: 180, maxY: 24, n: 8 };

function gx(g, t) { return g.x + t * g.w / (g.n - 1); }
// y position of a count v in a diagram g (0 at the bottom).
function gy(g, v) { return g.y + g.h - v * g.h / g.maxY; }
// Builds the SVG path of a band between an upper series and a lower series (filled area) over the first k points.
function band(g, upper, lower, k) { let d = ""; for (let t = 0; t < k; t++) { d += (t === 0 ? "M" : "L") + gx(g, t) + " " + gy(g, upper[t]); } for (let t = k - 1; t >= 0; t--) { d += "L" + gx(g, t) + " " + gy(g, lower[t]); } return d + "Z"; }

// Draws the axes, the grid and the caption of a diagram.
function axes(g, title, xLabels, yStep) { txt(g.x, g.y - 14, title, { size: 10.5, weight: 800 }); el("rect", { x: g.x, y: g.y, width: g.w, height: g.h, fill: "#fff", stroke: C.line }); for (let v = 0; v <= g.maxY; v += yStep) { el("line", { x1: g.x, y1: gy(g, v), x2: g.x + g.w, y2: gy(g, v), stroke: C.grid }); txt(g.x - 5, gy(g, v) + 3, String(v), { size: 8, fill: C.muted, anchor: "end" }); } xLabels.forEach(function (l, t) { if (l) { txt(gx(g, t), g.y + g.h + 11, l, { size: 7.5, fill: C.muted, anchor: "middle" }); } }); txt(g.x - 30, g.y + g.h / 2, "items (cumulative)", { size: 7.5, fill: C.muted, anchor: "middle" }).setAttribute("transform", "rotate(-90 " + (g.x - 30) + " " + (g.y + g.h / 2) + ")"); }

[[C.indigoT, C.indigo, "Ready (committed, not started)"], [C.rustT, C.rust, "In progress (started, not finished) = WIP"], [C.goldT, C.gold, "Review (generic team only)"], [C.tealT, C.teal, "Done (finished)"]].forEach(function (s, i) { el("rect", { x: 50 + i * 178, y: ly - 8, width: 12, height: 10, fill: s[0], stroke: s[1] }); txt(66 + i * 178, ly, s[2], { size: 8, fill: C.muted }); });

}
// Redraws Team Menu's diagram over the first k days: two bands, three lines, the end-of-day numbers.
function drawA(k) { layers.aBands.innerHTML = ""; layers.aLines.innerHTML = ""; const s = seriesA; if (k >= 2) { el("path", { d: band(A, s.committed, s.started, k), fill: C.indigoT }, layers.aBands); el("path", { d: band(A, s.started, s.finished, k), fill: C.rustT }, layers.aBands); el("path", { d: band(A, s.finished, s.finished.map(function () { return 0; }), k), fill: C.tealT }, layers.aBands); } el("path", { d: line(A, s.committed, k), fill: "none", stroke: C.indigo, "stroke-width": 2 }, layers.aLines); el("path", { d: line(A, s.started, k), fill: "none", stroke: C.rust, "stroke-width": 2 }, layers.aLines); el("path", { d: line(A, s.finished, k), fill: "none", stroke: C.teal, "stroke-width": 2 }, layers.aLines); const t = k - 1; [["committed", C.indigo], ["started", C.rust], ["finished", C.teal]].forEach(function (p) { el("circle", { cx: gx(A, t), cy: gy(A, s[p[0]][t]), r: 3, fill: p[1] }, layers.aLines); }); txt(gx(A, t) + 4, gy(A, s.committed[t]) - 6, "C " + s.committed[t] + " · S " + s.started[t] + " · F " + s.finished[t], { size: 7.5, fill: C.muted, parent: layers.aLines, anchor: t > 9 ? "end" : "start" }); }
// Draws the generic diagram over the first k weeks: four bands and four lines.
function drawB(k) { layers.bBands.innerHTML = ""; const w = WEEKS; const zero = w.done.map(function () { return 0; }); if (k >= 2) { el("path", { d: band(B, w.committed, w.started, k), fill: C.indigoT }, layers.bBands); el("path", { d: band(B, w.started, w.review, k), fill: C.rustT }, layers.bBands); el("path", { d: band(B, w.review, w.done, k), fill: C.goldT }, layers.bBands); el("path", { d: band(B, w.done, zero, k), fill: C.tealT }, layers.bBands); } [["committed", C.indigo], ["started", C.rust], ["review", C.gold], ["done", C.teal]].forEach(function (p) { el("path", { d: line(B, w[p[0]], k), fill: "none", stroke: p[1], "stroke-width": 2 }, layers.bBands); }); const t = k - 1; txt(gx(B, t) + (t > 5 ? -4 : 4), gy(B, w.committed[t]) - 6, "WIP " + (w.started[t] - w.review[t]) + " · done " + w.done[t], { size: 7.5, fill: C.muted, parent: layers.bBands, anchor: t > 5 ? "end" : "start" }); }
// Writes one checklist row (question, answer, what it points to) in the checklist frame.
function drawCheck(i, item, tag) { const y = 304 + i * 46; txt(26, y, "Q" + (i + 1) + "  " + item.q, { size: 8.8, weight: 700, parent: layers.check }); wrap(item.a, 150).forEach(function (l, k) { txt(44, y + 13 + k * 11, l, { size: 8.5, fill: C.muted, parent: layers.check }); }); txt(736, y, tag, { size: 8.8, weight: 800, fill: item.votes === "none" ? C.muted : (item.votes === "scrum" ? C.indigo : C.rust), anchor: "end", parent: layers.check }); }
// Builds the ordered list of steps.
function buildSteps() {
// Empties the list (needed by Restart).
steps.length = 0;
// Step 1: what the program will do.
steps.push(function () { return "Start · left: Team Menu's Sprint 1 cumulative flow diagram built one day at a time from the three dates of each card; right: a generic eight-week diagram with four states; bottom: the three questions that decide the method."; });
// Step 2: inputs.
steps.push(function () { return "Inputs · four cards (committed, started, finished), window Oct 12 → 25; generic team: weekly cumulative counts for committed, started, review and done; a checklist of three questions. cumulative(day) counts, per state, the cards that entered it on or before the day — that is all a CFD is."; });
// Steps 3 to 16: one per day of Team Menu's diagram.
for (let n = 0; n < NDAYS; n++) { steps.push(function () { const s = dayN(n); const c = cumulative(s); seriesA.committed.push(c.committed); seriesA.started.push(c.started); seriesA.finished.push(c.finished); drawA(n + 1); const ready = c.committed - c.started, wip = c.started - c.finished; let note = ""; if (n === 0) { note = " · the committed line jumps to 4 at the Sprint Planning; two cards started the same day."; } if (s === "2026-10-15") { note = " · the In progress band is at its widest: 4 items = the whole Sprint content."; } if (c.finished > (n > 0 ? seriesA.finished[n - 1] : 0)) { note = " · the finished line rises by one: a card crossed the delivery point."; } if (n === NDAYS - 1) { note = " · the finished line has been flat since Oct 22: nothing finished in the last three days while story 4 stayed open."; } return label(s) + " · entered: committed " + c.committed + ", started " + c.started + ", finished " + c.finished + " → bands: Ready " + ready + ", In progress " + wip + ", Done " + c.finished + note; }); }
// Step 17: reading 1 — thickness.
steps.push(function () { const t = 3; el("line", { x1: gx(A, t), y1: gy(A, 4), x2: gx(A, t), y2: gy(A, 0), stroke: C.ink, "stroke-width": 1.5, "stroke-dasharray": "3 2" }, layers.aRead); txt(gx(A, t) + 4, gy(A, 2) + 3, "thickness = 4 = WIP", { size: 8, weight: 800, parent: layers.aRead }); return "Reading 1 · THICKNESS of the In progress band, read vertically: on Oct 15 the band spans 4 items — the WIP of that day (the peak of Lesson 3's daily counts)."; });

These are the lead times of Lesson 3, read on the picture instead of computed."; });
// Step 19: reading 3 — slope.
steps.push(function () { txt(gx(A, 13) - 2, gy(A, 0.12), "slope of the finished line: 3 items / 14 d ≈ 0.21 per day", { size: 8, weight: 800, fill: C.teal, anchor: "end", parent: layers.aRead }); return "Reading 3 · SLOPE of the finished line, the bottom line: it rises by one item on Oct 16, 19 and 22 — 3 items in 14 days, about 0.21 per day — and is flat since Oct 22. The slope is the throughput."; });
// Steps 20 to 27: the generic diagram week by week.
for (let k = 1; k <= 8; k++) { steps.push(function () { drawB(k); const w = WEEKS; const wip = w.started[k - 1] - w.review[k - 1]; const doneThisWeek = w.done[k - 1] - (k > 1 ? w.done[k - 2] : 0); let note = ""; if (k === 4) { note = " · so far the finished line keeps pace: 2 items per week."; } if (k === 5) { note = " · from here the finished line slows to 1 per week while the In progress band keeps growing: the signal of a bottleneck."; } return "Generic team · week " + k + " · committed " + w.committed[k - 1] + ", started " + w.started[k - 1] + ", in review " + w.review[k - 1] + ", done " + w.done[k - 1] + " → In progress band " + wip + " items, finished this week " + doneThisWeek + note; }); }
// Step 28: naming the bottleneck.
steps.push(function () { el("rect", { x: gx(B, 4) - 2, y: gy(B, WEEKS.started[7]) - 2, width: gx(B, 7) - gx(B, 4) + 4, height: gy(B, WEEKS.review[4]) - gy(B, WEEKS.started[7]) + 4, fill: "none", stroke: C.rust, "stroke-width": 2, "stroke-dasharray": "4 3" }, layers.bRead); txt(gx(B, 4), gy(B, 22), "widening band = bottleneck", { size: 8, weight: 800, fill: C.rust, parent: layers.bRead }); return "Bottleneck · the In progress band widens from 1 item (week 1) to 12 (week 8) while the finished line slows from 2 to 1 per week; the Ready and Review bands stay thin. The state whose band widens is where work accumulates: In progress. Three actions (Lesson 2): lower its limit, swarm on the oldest items, find what is blocked — not 'start more'."; });

CHECKLIST.forEach(function (item, i) { steps.push(function () { const tag = item.votes === "scrum" ? "→ keep Scrum" : (item.votes === "kanban-practices" ? Memo:\n     " + MEMO.join("\n     "); });

steps.push(function () { return "Done · the left diagram is Lesson 3's table drawn; the right one is the Companion's drill; the memo is the five sentences each team writes in the studio. Try: replace CARDS by your own Sprint 1 cards, or change WEEKS so that the Review band is the one that widens, and read where the bottleneck moved."; });
// End of buildSteps.
}
// Restart: stops, clears the log, redraws the empty frame, rebuilds the steps and returns to step 0.
function restart() { pause(); next = 0; layers = {}; logBox.innerHTML = ""; drawFrame(); buildSteps(); counter.textContent = "Step 0 / " + steps.length; runBtn.textContent = "▶ Start"; }
// Writes one numbered line in the execution window, highlights it and scrolls down to it.
function log(text) { const prev = logBox.querySelector(".now"); if (prev) { prev.classList.remove("now"); } const d = document.createElement("div"); d.className = "now"; d.textContent = String(next).padStart(2, "0") + " │ " + text; logBox.appendChild(d); logBox.scrollTop = logBox.scrollHeight; }
// Runs the next step, writes its result, updates the counter, and stops by itself after the last step.
function stepOnce() { if (next >= steps.length) { pause(); return; } const text = steps[next](); next += 1; log(text); counter.textContent = "Step " + next + " / " + steps.length; if (next >= steps.length) { pause(); runBtn.textContent = "✓ Finished"; } }
// Starts (or resumes) the automatic run: one step now, then one step every DELAY milliseconds.
function start() { if (next >= steps.length) { return; } runBtn.textContent = "⏸ Pause"; stepOnce(); if (next < steps.length) { timer = setInterval(stepOnce, DELAY); } }
// Pauses the automatic run; the next Start continues from exactly the same step.
function pause() { clearInterval(timer); timer = null; if (next < steps.length) { runBtn.textContent = "▶ Start"; } }
// Copies SOURCE to the clipboard; if the browser blocks the Clipboard API (Application Programming Interface), a hidden text area is used instead.
function copyCode() { const b = document.getElementById("copy"); const done = function () { b.textContent = "✓ Copied"; setTimeout(function () { b.textContent = "⧉ Copy code"; }, 1500); }; const fallback = function () { const t = document.createElement("textarea"); t.value = SOURCE; document.body.appendChild(t); t.select(); document.execCommand("copy"); t.remove(); done(); }; if (navigator.clipboard && window.isSecureContext) { navigator.clipboard.writeText(SOURCE).then(done, fallback); } else { fallback(); } }
// Serializes the drawing as it is now into a self-contained SVG text (with the XML namespace and a white background).
function svgText() { const clone = svg.cloneNode(true); clone.setAttribute("xmlns", NS); const bg = document.createElementNS(NS, "rect"); bg.setAttribute("width", "100%"); bg.setAttribute("height", "100%"); bg.setAttribute("fill", "#FFFFFF"); clone.insertBefore(bg, clone.firstChild); return '<?xml version="1.0" encoding="UTF-8"?>\n' + new XMLSerializer().serializeToString(clone); }
// Triggers a browser download of the given text or blob under the given file name.
function download(name, data, type) { const blob = data instanceof Blob ? data : new Blob([data], { type: type }); const url = URL.createObjectURL(blob); const a = document.createElement("a"); a.href = url; a.download = name; document.body.appendChild(a); a.click(); a.remove(); setTimeout(function () { URL.revokeObjectURL(url); }, 1000); }
// Download SVG button: saves the current drawing as a vector file.
document.getElementById("dlsvg").addEventListener("click", function () { download("ex4_cfd_and_method_chooser.svg", svgText(), "image/svg+xml"); });
// Download PNG button: draws the current SVG on a hidden canvas at double resolution, then saves it as a picture file.
document.getElementById("dlpng").addEventListener("click", function () { const img = new Image(); const url = URL.createObjectURL(new Blob([svgText()], { type: "image/svg+xml" })); img.onload = function () { const c = document.createElement("canvas"); c.width = 760 * 2; c.height = 520 * 2; const g = c.getContext("2d"); g.fillStyle = "#FFFFFF"; g.fillRect(0, 0, c.width, c.height); g.drawImage(img, 0, 0, c.width, c.height); URL.revokeObjectURL(url); c.toBlob(function (b) { download("ex4_cfd_and_method_chooser.png", b, "image/png"); }, "image/png"); }; img.src = url; });
// Start/Pause button: pauses if the program is running, otherwise starts or resumes it.
runBtn.addEventListener("click", function () { if (timer) { pause(); } else { start(); } });
// Next-step button: works only while paused, so the class sets the pace.
document.getElementById("stepBtn").addEventListener("click", function () { if (!timer) { stepOnce(); } });
// Restart button.
document.getElementById("reset").addEventListener("click", restart);
// Copy-code button.
document.getElementById("copy").addEventListener("click", copyCode);
// Draws the starting state as soon as the page is loaded.
restart();
// End of the program.
</script>
<!-- End of the visible page. -->
</body>

Step by step — what the program does

  1. Inputs. CARDS holds Team Menu's four cards with their three dates; WEEKS holds the eight weekly cumulative counts of the generic team (committed, started, reviewed, finished); CHECKLIST holds the three questions about the kind of work and Team Menu's answers.
  2. Cumulative counts. cumulative(day) counts, for each state, how many cards have entered it on or before the day; the first fourteen steps add one day each to the diagram, drawing the three lines and filling the two bands — Ready on top, In progress in the middle, Done at the bottom.
  3. Reading the picture. After the last day, three steps draw the three readings on the diagram: a vertical bracket on October 15 (thickness = 4 = WIP), three horizontal arrows from the committed line to the finished line (4, 7, 10 days), and the slope of the finished line (3 items in 14 days).
  4. The generic diagram. The next steps draw the eight-week diagram week by week; when the In progress band grows faster than the finished line, the log says so and the band is highlighted as the bottleneck, with the three actions of Lesson 2.
  5. The checklist. The last steps answer the three questions for Team Menu — plannable into a goal? stakeholders want a rhythm? queues and too much started at once? — and print the method that follows (Scrumban) with the five-sentence memo.
  6. Controls. Start / Pause / Next step / Restart / Copy / ⤓ SVG / ⤓ PNG, as in Example 1. Pause on October 15 and ask the class to read the WIP off the picture before the log prints it.
  7. Try it. In the copied code, replace the four cards by your team's Sprint 1 cards and press Restart to get your own diagram; then change the WEEKS numbers so that the Review band, not the In progress band, is the one that widens, and read where the bottleneck moved.

Buttons: ▶ Start / ⏸ Pause (resumes where it stopped), ⏭ Next step, ↺ Restart, ⧉ Copy code, ⤓ SVG / ⤓ PNG (download the picture as it is now); every step is written in the execution window. A comment line precedes every line of code. Educational example, provided as is for your own study (Legal Notice, sections 4.2 and 11).

Flash-cards · Lesson 4 · click a card to flip it

Card 4.1 · question

What does a cumulative flow diagram plot?

Answer

For every day, the cumulative number of items that have entered each state — committed, started, finished — as stacked bands; lines only rise or stay flat.

Card 4.2 · question

The three readings of a CFD?

Answer

Vertical thickness of a band = items in that state (the middle band is the WIP); horizontal distance between the top and bottom lines = approximate lead time; slope of the bottom line = throughput.

Card 4.3 · question

A band widens while the bottom line goes flat. Diagnosis and action?

Answer

A bottleneck: items enter that state faster than they leave it, and nothing is being finished. Lower the WIP limit, swarm on finishing, look for the blocked items.

Card 4.4 · question

What is a Service Level Expectation?

Answer

A forecast of how long a work item should take from started to finished, with two parts — a period and a probability — based on historical cycle times: '85 % within 8 days'. A forecast, not a promise.

Card 4.5 · question

Scrum versus Kanban in one line each?

Answer

Scrum: a framework with prescribed accountabilities, five events in a time-box, three artifacts; work enters at Sprint Planning. Kanban: a strategy for flow with no prescribed roles, events or artifacts; continuous pull, explicit WIP limits, flow measures.

Card 4.6 · question

What is Scrumban, and who named it?

Answer

A Scrum team that adopts Kanban's pull, WIP limits and flow measures while keeping all of Scrum — named by Corey Ladas (2008–2009); the same combination Scrum.org describes in its Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams.

Self-check · Lesson 4

Formative · not counted toward grades

Four single-answer questions (MCQ) and two multiple-answer questions (MSQ — the number of correct options is given in round brackets). Choose, then reveal; every option has an explanation.

1. On a cumulative flow diagram, the vertical thickness of the In progress band on a given day shows…MCQ · one correct answer
💡 Up is WIP, across is lead time.
2. On a CFD the In progress band widens from 4 to 10 over three weeks while the finished line stays flat. What is the diagnosis?MCQ · one correct answer
💡 Compare how fast items enter the band with how fast they leave it.
3. Which sentence is a Service Level Expectation as the Kanban Guide defines it?MCQ · one correct answer
💡 Two parts: a period and a probability, based on historical cycle time.
4. A support desk receives requests continuously, each independent of the others, and cannot wait for a planning day. Which method fits best, and why?MCQ · one correct answer
💡 The criterion is the kind of work.
5. Which statements correctly describe Kanban, as opposed to Scrum? (3)MSQ · 3 correct answers
💡 What Kanban prescribes and what it leaves open.
6. Which statements about Scrumban are correct? (2)MSQ · 2 correct answers
💡 Who named it, and what it keeps.
