Terms to learn — all four lessons

TermDefinitionWhere
Kanban (card)In the Toyota Production System, a visual card attached to a container that travels back to the preceding process as the order to make one more — nothing is produced until a card says something was used.Lesson 1
Toyota Production System (TPS)Toyota's manufacturing system, built from the 1950s on two pillars: jidoka (stop at an abnormality) and Just-in-Time (make only what is needed, when it is needed, in the amount needed).Lesson 1
PullWork is produced or started because the downstream process signalled capacity and demand; the opposite of push, where upstream hands work on regardless of capacity.Lesson 1
Kanban MethodDavid J. Anderson's method (2010) for defining, managing and improving services that deliver knowledge work; six general practices: visualize, limit WIP, manage flow, make policies explicit, implement feedback loops, improve collaboratively and evolve experimentally.Lesson 1
Kanban GuideThe free guide of John Coleman and Daniel Vacanti (edition 2025.5): Kanban as a strategy for optimizing the flow of value through a process; three practices: define and visualize a workflow, actively manage items, improve the workflow.Lesson 1
Definition of Workflow (DoW)The six elements a Kanban system must define: work items; when an item is started and finished; the states between them; how WIP is controlled; explicit policies per state; a Service Level Expectation.Lesson 1
Work itemOne unit of value moving through the workflow — in this course, one user story (or a spike, marked as a different kind of card).Lesson 1
StateOne step of the workflow between started and finished; shown as a column of the board.Lesson 1
Explicit policyA written rule at the top of a column: what must be true for a card to enter, what is done there, and how many cards may be there at once.Lesson 1
Commitment pointThe line on the board where the team decides it will do the item (here: entering Ready); the lead-time clock starts there.Lesson 1
Delivery pointThe line on the board where the item is usable by the people it is for (here: entering Done, after all Definition of Done checks); the clock stops there.Lesson 1
Kanban boardThe visible form of the Definition of Workflow: columns for states, cards for work items, policies and limits written on the columns, two dates on every card.Lesson 1
WIP (Work In Progress)The number of work items started but not finished (Kanban Guide) — a count of items, not of hours, points or people.Lesson 2
Cost of WIPWhat every started-but-unfinished item consumes: attention, ageing of the information it was based on, and delayed feedback for the people who wait for it.Lesson 2
Average lead time under shared capacityThree equal stories, three days each: start all at once → lead times 9, 9, 9 (average 9); one at a time → 3, 6, 9 (average 6), same total work, first delivery three times earlier.Lesson 2
Switching costThe time and accuracy lost each time a person changes task (goal shifting and rule activation — Rubinstein, Meyer & Evans, 2001, summarized by the APA); it grows with the complexity of the tasks.Lesson 2
Stop starting, start finishingThe Kanban community's sentence for the two effects above (title of Arne Roock's 2012 booklet): with limited capacity, finishing before starting shortens the average wait.Lesson 2
WIP limitA number written on a column — or on the whole board between the commitment point and the delivery point — that the team agrees not to exceed; an explicit policy, changed only by decision.Lesson 2
Neither above nor belowThe Kanban Guide's rule for the limit: above it, the queueing cost returns; below it, people wait for a slot while they could help finish.Lesson 2
First limitAtlassian's advice: observe how many items each state really holds, choose as a team, keep it long enough to see the effect; for a small team, a limit below the number of people.Lesson 2
Full columnThe signal to finish rather than start: pair on the oldest card, take the waiting Review, remove the blocker, or improve the policy — never idle, never a punishment.Lesson 2
SwarmingSeveral members working on one item to finish it, the usual answer to a full column.Lesson 2
Owner of the countThe member who checks the WIP count at each Daily Scrum (Team Menu: Amira); the decision to change the limit remains the team's.Lesson 2
Cycle timeThe elapsed time between when a work item started (entered In progress) and when it finished (entered Done) — Kanban Guide; in this course the difference of the two dates, in calendar days.Lesson 3
Work item ageThe elapsed time between when a work item started and the current date — the cycle-time clock read before the item has finished; the number that says which card to help today.Lesson 3
Lead timeThe elapsed time from the commitment point (the card entered Ready) to the delivery point (Done) — Kanban University vocabulary; the clock the person who was promised the item experiences.Lesson 3
Elapsed timeCalendar time including the days nobody touched the card, because the people who wait experience calendar time; never 'active hours'.Lesson 3
Counting conventionThe rule written in the Definition of Workflow for turning two dates into days; this course: finish date minus start date (Monday → Friday = 4 days).Lesson 3
From when?The question to ask before accepting any flow number: which point starts the clock — commitment, start, or now.Lesson 3
ThroughputThe number of work items finished per unit of time — an exact count of items, per day, per week or per Sprint, the period stated.Lesson 3
Throughput versus velocityThroughput counts finished items; velocity sums the story points of finished items; they answer different questions and are never converted into each other.Lesson 3
Little's Law (1961)L = λW: in a stable queue the average number of items in the system equals the arrival rate times the average time in the system (John D. C. Little, Operations Research).Lesson 3
Little's Law, flow formAverage WIP = throughput × average cycle time; average cycle time = average WIP ÷ throughput; units must match (items, items per day, days).Lesson 3
Conditions of the flow form (Vacanti, 2015)Arrival rate equals departure rate · every item that enters eventually leaves · WIP about the same at the start and the end of the period · the average age of WIP neither grows nor shrinks · consistent units.Lesson 3
Average WIPThe mean of the daily counts of items in progress over the period — Team Menu: 31 card-days ÷ 14 days ≈ 2.2 items.Lesson 3
Less WIP, shorter cycle timeAt the same throughput, Little's Law gives a shorter average cycle time for a lower average WIP: the limit of Lesson 2 shortens waiting, not work.Lesson 3
Cumulative Flow Diagram (CFD)A chart of the cumulative number of items that have entered each state, day by day, drawn as stacked bands — finished at the bottom, in progress above, committed on top.Lesson 4
Band thicknessThe vertical distance across a band on a given day = the number of items in that state that day; the middle band is the WIP.Lesson 4
Horizontal distanceThe distance between the top line (committed) and the bottom line (finished) at a given height = the approximate average lead time of the items committed that day.Lesson 4
Slope of the finished lineItems finished per day = the throughput; a flat stretch means nothing was finished.Lesson 4
Widening band / bottleneckA band whose top line rises faster than its bottom line: items enter that state faster than they leave it — the place to look first.Lesson 4
Service Level Expectation (SLE)A forecast of how long a work item should take from started to finished, with two parts — a period and a probability — based on historical cycle time (Kanban Guide): '85 % within 8 days'.Lesson 4
Provisional SLEAn SLE written from very few cycle times (Team Menu: three), kept in pencil and recomputed as data accumulates; a forecast, never a promise.Lesson 4
Scrum (framework)Three accountabilities, five events in a Sprint of one month or less, three artifacts with commitments, a Sprint Goal fixed for the Sprint; work enters at Sprint Planning (Scrum Guide 2020).Lesson 4
Kanban (strategy / method)No prescribed roles, events or artifacts; continuous pull when there is capacity; explicit WIP limits and policies; measures: WIP, throughput, work item age, cycle time, SLE.Lesson 4
ScrumbanCorey Ladas's name (2008–2009) for a Scrum team that adopts Kanban's pull, WIP limits and flow measures while keeping Scrum — all of Scrum plus the practices of this hour.Lesson 4
Kind of workThe criterion for choosing: plannable into a time-boxed goal with stakeholders who want a rhythm → Scrum; continuous, unpredictable, independent items → Kanban; a Scrum team that wants flow without losing its rhythm → Scrumban.Lesson 4
Decision memoFive sentences, each with a reason, ending with a method and a date for reviewing the decision (the studio's last block today).Lesson 4

Organizations, guides and papers

  1. The Kanban Guide — kanbanguides.org (Coleman & Vacanti, edition 2025.5) — The free guide that defines the four flow measures of this course — WIP, throughput, work item age, cycle time — the Definition of Workflow and the Service Level Expectation; its three practices are the ground of Lessons 1 to 4.
    https://kanbanguides.org/the-kanban-guide/
  2. The Kanban Guide — PDF of edition 2025.5 — The same text as a PDF (May 1, 2025), licensed under Creative Commons Attribution-ShareAlike.
    https://kanbanguides.org/the-kanban-guide/2025.5/pdf/kanban-guide.v2025.5.en.pdf
  3. Kanban University — The Official Guide to the Kanban Method — The vocabulary of David J. Anderson's Kanban Method (2010): the six general practices, the commitment point, the delivery point, lead time, pull system, WIP limits.
    https://kanban.university/kanban-guide/
  4. David J. Anderson — A Brief History of Kanban for Knowledge Work (2014, updated 2026) — The author's own account of the first knowledge-work kanban system (Microsoft XIT, 2004), Corbis (2006–2007) and the 2010 book.
    https://djaa.com/brief-history-kanban-knowledge-work/
  5. Toyota Motor Corporation — Toyota Production System — Toyota's official page on the two pillars, jidoka and Just-in-Time, and on the people who built the system (Sakichi Toyoda, Kiichiro Toyoda, Taiichi Ohno, Eiji Toyoda).
    https://global.toyota/en/company/vision-and-philosophy/production-system/
  6. Toyota UK Magazine — Kanban, Toyota Production System guide — Toyota's own explanation of the kanban card: a system that conveys information between processes and orders parts as they are used up.
    https://mag.toyota.co.uk/kanban-toyota-production-system/
  7. The Scrum Guide 2020 — scrumguides.org — The official, free definition of Scrum (Schwaber & Sutherland, November 2020): the reference for every comparison of Lesson 4.
    https://scrumguides.org/scrum-guide.html
  8. Scrum.org — Kanban Guide for Scrum Teams — How a Scrum Team adds the flow practices of Kanban without changing Scrum; the four flow metrics are the same as the Kanban Guide's.
    https://www.scrum.org/resources/kanban-guide-scrum-teams
  9. Modus Cooperandi — Scrumban, by Corey Ladas — The publisher's page for the essays (2008) and the book (2009) that named Scrumban: a Scrum team adopting Kanban's pull, limits and flow.
    https://moduscooperandi.com/modus-cooperandi/blog/scrumban-by-corey-ladas
  10. John D. C. Little — A Proof for the Queuing Formula: L = λW (1961) — The original paper of Little's Law, Operations Research 9(3), 383–387: the average number of items in a system equals the arrival rate times the average time in the system.
    https://doi.org/10.1287/opre.9.3.383
  11. J. D. C. Little — Little's Law as Viewed on Its 50th Anniversary (2011) — Little's own review of the law fifty years later, including the conditions under which it holds.
    https://pubsonline.informs.org/doi/10.1287/opre.1110.0940
  12. ProKanban.org — The Kanban Pocket Guide, Chapter 6: The Basic Metrics of Flow (Daniel Vacanti, 2024) — Why the four flow metrics are counted in elapsed time and exact item counts, and why work item age matters while an item is still open.
    https://prokanban.org/blog/the-kanban-pocket-guide-chapter-6-the-basic-metrics-of-flow
  13. Atlassian — Putting the 'flow' back in workflow with WIP limits (Dan Radigan) — A free article on what WIP limits are, why they reduce context switching and expose blockers, and how to set a first limit.
    https://www.atlassian.com/agile/kanban/wip-limits
  14. Atlassian — What is a kanban board? (Max Rehkopf) — The five elements of a board — visual signals, columns, WIP limits, a commitment point, a delivery point — with lead time measured between the two points.
    https://www.atlassian.com/agile/kanban/boards
  15. American Psychological Association — Multitasking: Switching costs (2006) — The research summary behind Lesson 2: goal shifting and rule activation, and why repeated switching costs time and accuracy (Rubinstein, Meyer & Evans, 2001).
    https://www.apa.org/topics/research/multitasking
  16. Kanban Tool library — Stop Starting, Start Finishing! (Arne Roock, 2012) — The short booklet that gave the Kanban community its best-known sentence about WIP.
    https://kanbantool.com/kanban-library/books/stop-starting-start-finishing
  17. Stephen Denning — stevedenning.com — Author of The Age of Agile (2018), the required text; Chapter 6 is this week's reading.
    https://www.stevedenning.com/
  18. VitalSource Bookshelf — vitalsource.com — Where your e-copy of The Age of Agile lives.
    https://www.vitalsource.com/
  19. Blackboard — blackboard.com — The course platform: attendance, CQ2, the Lab 04 hand-in next week, the Q&A board.
    https://www.blackboard.com/
